parties:
Abdur Razzak ------ Petitioner.
Vs.
Ahila Khatun & Ors ------ Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
Muhammad Ansar Ali, J.: This Rule at the instance of the Plaintiff-Petitioner is directed against the judgment and decree dated 5.9.88 passed by the Judge-in-Charge of the Court of the Additional District Judge, Rangpur, in Other Appeal No. 116 of 1987, affirming those dated 18.4.87 passed by the Assistant Judge, Mithapukur Upazila, in Other Suit No. 127 of 1983, for partition. 

2. Plaintiff's case was that the suit-land originally belonged to one Paklu Sheikh and his name was recorded in the last C.S. Khatian and the total area of the suit-land was 3.95 acres out of which Peklu Sheikh sold 1.01 acres to one Abdur Rahim and retained 2.94 acres in his possession; that Peklu Sheikh died leaving behind one wife Bachachu Mui, five sons, Kalo, Nalto, Jalo, Nalo and Ayenuddin and four daughters, Basiron, Nasiron, Mahiron and Kafiran, that on the death of the said Peklu Sheikh, his aforesaid heirs inherited the lands. Thereafter, Bachchu Mui died leaving behind only two sons, Kalu and Nalo and 4 daughters as named above; then Mohirun died leaving behind her husband Osman and 2 sons Rustom and Sekandar; that Rustom and Osman, out of their share of the suit-lands, sold 17½ acre of land to Jalo Sk. and his son by a registered deed dated 19.3.66 Meanwhile, Jalo Sheikh, out of his share for an area of .36½ acre of land, transferred .35 acre of the suit-land to his son Majibar and daughter Shahida Khatoon by a registered deed of Heba-bil-Ewaz dated 20.8.60; that the defendant No. 11 Shahida Khatoon sold and transferred .17½ acre of her land to the Plaintiff-petitioner by a registered deed of sale dated 22.5.74 and Defendant No. 9 Majibar sold .17½ acre of land to the Plaintiff by another registered deed of sale dated 25.3.74 and, thereafter, Sekandar Ali, defendant No. 33, son of Mohiran, also sold .08 acre of land to the Plaintiff by another registered deed of sale dated 7.6.80; thus the Plaintiff-petitioner in all acquired .43 acre of land and became a co-sharer in the suit jote; that the further case of the Plaintiff is that the Plaintiff reconeyed . 17½ acre of land to the vendor Mojibur and then Mojibur sold out the same to one Awaf and then again the said Awaf sold out the same to the Plaintiff; that the plaintiff has been in ejmali possession of the suit lands, but there has been inconvenience and trouble with respect to his ejmali possession. Hence, he requested the defendants to make an amicable partition of the suit lands, but they refused to do so. The Plaintiff therefore filed the present suit for partition.

3. The Defendants Nos. 44-46 and 48-49 contested the suit by filing 2 separate written statements. Their written statements are almost of similar nature. In both the written statements, it was alleged that the suit was not maintainable in the present form and the same was barred by limitation and that the Plaintiff was not a co-sharer in the suit jote and there was defect of parties and, further, some material allegations made in the plaint were denied by the Defendants Their case, inter-alia, was that the said Jalo Sheikh did not transfer any land to his son Mojibur and daughter Shahida, Defendants Nos. 9 and 11 respectively, by any Heba-Bil-Ewaz deed and that the alleged Heba-bil-Ewaz deed was false, concocted, collusive and not genuine; further case of the Defendants, as that Jalo purchased .17½ acre of land from one Osman and Rustom, the legal heirs of Majibur and Mosiran and that Jalo inherited .36½ Acre of land and further kabala purchased .08% acre of land and thus became a co-sharer of .45½ acre of land and that the alleged kabala deeds of Majibur and Shahida in favour of the plaintiff are collusive and void; that the Defendant No. 33 Sekandar executed a fake and void deed for .08 acre of land in favour of the Plaintiff as he had no title and possession in the same; that Malo transferred .34 acre of land to his wife by Heba-bil-Ewaz deed dated 20.2.60 and then Malo and his wife sold out their share to Defendant No. 49, but by mistake mentioned .44 acre of and instead of . 63½  acre of land, that Malo sold .35 acre of land on 24.9.52 and Basiron and Kafiron sold .50 acre on 8.2.50 to one Abdur Rahim @ Jomser, and after the dath of Abdur Rahim @ Jomser the said land was inherited by his son Kinauddin and five daughters. Thereafter, by purchase from different co-sharers, the Defendants Nos. 48 and 49 acquired in all 1.13 acre of land for which they also prayed for saham and Defendant No. 54 Jonab Ali became a Co-Plaintiff in the suit and he also prayed for saham for his .30½ acre of land; the learned Munsif, now Assistant Judge, framed 5 issues for disposal of the suit. The first one was (1) Whether the suit was maintainable (2) Whether the suit was barred by limitation; (3) Whether there was defect of parties in the suit? (4) Whether the Plaintiff was a co-sharer on the basis of his Kabala purchase and whether he had title and possession in the suit land; and; lastly (5) Whether the Plaintiff was entitled to any other relief or reliefs. 

4. On behalf of the Plaintiffs, 3 witnesses were examined and on behalf of the Defendants 4 witnesses were examined, including Defendant No. 49 Yasin Ali. Both the sides filed some documents in support of the respective cases including a certified copy of the alleged Heba-bil Ewaz deed dated 20.8.60. After hearing both the sides and having considered the evidence on record, the learned Assistant Judge decided issues Nos. 1, 2 and 3 in favour of the Plaintiff and the main issues, namely, issues Nos. 4 and 5 against him and, accordingly, dismissed the suit on contest as against the contesting Defendants and ex-parte against the rest without any costs, by his judgment and decree dated 18.4.87. 

5. Being aggrieved by the same, the Plaintiff filed Other Appeal No. 116 of 1987 to the District Judge, Rangpur, and the same was heard by the Judge-in-Charge of the Court of the Additional District Judge, Rangpur, who, after hearing both the sides and on consideration of the evidence on record, dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court by his judgment and decree dated 5.9.88. Being aggrieved by the same, the Plaintiff-petitioner moved this Court in revision and obtained the present Rule. 

6. Mr. Md. Fazlul Karim, the learned Senior Advocate, appeared for the Plaintiff-petitioner in support of the Rule and Mr. Akram Hossain Amin the learned Advocate appeared for the Defendant Opposite Parties Nos. 1, 2, 3 and 5 by filing separate Vokalatnamas to oppose the Rule. 

7. Mr. Md. Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, has seriously assailed the judgment and decree of both the Courts below. He has firstly contended that the learned Additional District Judge-in-Charge has committed an error of law apparent on the face of the record in dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and decree of the trial Court by which the Plaintiff's suit for partition was dismissed on an illegal finding that, the Heba-bil-Ewaz deed executed by Jalo Sheikh with regard to .35 acre of the suit-lands in favour of his son Mojibor Mia and daughter Shehida Khatoon was false and not genuine and the same was not acted upon and consequently the Plaintiff's vendors had no right, title and authority to transfer the said.35 acre of land in his favour by the alleged two separate sale-deeds dated 25.3.74 and 22.5.74 and that the said vendors as well as the Plaintiff acquired no right, title or interest and possession over the suit-lands. The learned Advocate for the Petitioner has further submitted that the Courts below, without giving due and proper consideration to the evidence on record, both oral and documentary, have arrived at wrong conclusion with regard to the title and possession of the Plaintiff in the suit lands and as a result, there has been a failure of justice. His next contention is that the Courts below committed and error of law in not holding that the Plaintiff is entitled to get the partition of the suit-land even assuming, but not conceding, that the Plaintiff was out of possession. He has further argued that the learned Additional District Judge-in-Charge on misreading of facts and evidence on record erroneously held that the Plaintiffs purchase of the suit-lands was hit by Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, as the purchase of the suit-lands had taken place during pendency of the suit.

8. Mr. Akram Hossain Amin, the learned Advocate for the contesting Opposite Parties, on the other hand, has submitted that the submission of the learned Advocate for the Petitioner on the 1st. point is not based on the evidence on record. The Judgments of the Courts below clearly show that on the question of the genuineness of the Heba-bil-Ewaz deed, both the Courts below, on proper consideration of the evidence on record, have come to a concurrent finding that the alleged Heba-bil-Ewaz deed is a fake and fraudulent one and the same has not been acted upon at any time. The finding on the question of genuineness of a document, namely, the Heba-bil-Ewaz, in the instant suit is, a finding of fact which has been arrived at by both the Courts concurrently, on proper and correct appreciation and consideration of the materials on record, having given elaborate reasoning and that being the position, this Court, in revision, cannot go into such a question of fact unless the Plaintiff- petitioner is able to show that such concurrent finding of fact is a perverse one or based on no evidence or on misreading of evidence. I have gone through the judgments of both the Courts below. The certified copy of the alleged Heba-bil-Ewaz deed has been produced by the Plaintiff which has been marked as Ext. 'X'. In order to prove the said deed, the Plaintiff himself as P.W.1 is the only witness. His other 2 witnesses have not said anything about the disputed Hiba-bil-Ewaz deed. Neither the scribe of the alleged Hiba-bil-Ewaz deed, nor any of the witnesses of the said deed has been examined by the Plaintiff and further, the alleged recipients of the Heba-bil-Ewaz deed, namely, Majibor Mia and Shahida Khatoon, though have been made parties in the instant suit and are alive, have not been examined by the Plaintiff, as witnesses to prove the genuineness of the disputed Heba-bil-Ewaz deed. Both the Courts below appear to have considered different aspects of the matter, namely, as to why the names of Majibor Mia and Shahida Khatoon, the alleged vendors of the Plaintiff, were not recorded in the R.S. Khatian, which was still appearing in the name of Jalo Sheikh, the original owner and again if the Plaintiff could really acquire title over the disputed .35 acre of the suit-land by purchase from Majibor and Shahida, how the same-land could be transferred by the same vendor to some other persons subsequently. It appears that the appellate Court further considered other aspects of the matter as to how one of the recipients of the alleged Heba-bil-Ewaz Majibor Mia being a minor at the time of the alleged Heba-bil- Ewaz could pay the consideration i.e. ewaz to the doner and what was the source of his income. In this connection, reference may be made to the case of Meherchand Banu Vs. Saimuallh and ors reported in 22 DLR (HC) at page 316 wherein it has been observed:- 

"In the case of Hiba-bil-Ewaz actual delivery of possession is not necessary. Payment of consideration to the doner and the bonafide intention of the donor to divest himself in present of the property and to confer it upon the donee are the necessary ingredients to give effect to a valid transfer under the deeds of Hiba-bil-Ewaz. 

9. The said ingredients could not be established by the Plaintiff in the instant suit. Further, another vital question has been considered by the lower appellate Court in its judgment and that is the failure of the Plaintiff to produce the original of the said Heba-bil-Ewaz deed which was supposed to have been obtained by him from his vendors Majibor and Shahida at the time of his purchase of the suit lands from them. In this regard, nothing has been stated in the Plaint nor any explanation given and also no evidence has been led to show that the original deed of Hiba-bil-Ewaz was lost or destroyed. It has, therefore, been contended by the learned Advocate for the Defendant Opposite Parties that the certified copy of the alleged Heba-bil-Ewaz deed was hit by Section 65 of the Evidence Act and the same cannot be taken into consideration to prove the alleged acquisition of .35 acre of land by the vendors of the Plaintiff, namely, Mojibur Mia and Shahida. In this connection, we may look into the provision of Section 65 of the Evidence Act and at the same time some decision of the superior Court, one in the case of Emmanucle Grech Vs. Antonie Grech and others reported in 6 DLR(P.C.) 598, wherein it has been laid down, inter alia, that secondary evidence to prove the contents of a document is not admissible until there is proof of its execution and subsequent loss or destruction. In the instant case, to prove the execution and the contents of the alleged deed, there is not only want of reliable evidence but there is no iota of evidence on the record to show that the original of the said deed was either lost or destroyed. Hence, the Courts below rightly and correctly found that the Plaintiff failed to prove his acquisition of .35 acre of land by purchase from his vendors Majibor Mia and Shahida Khatoon, who alleged to have acquired the same by virtue of the alleged Heba-bil-Ewaz from their father Jalo Sheikh. Thus, I find no substance in the first contention of the learned Advocate for the Petitioner on the point of genuineness and propriety of the alleged Heba-bil-Ewaz. Of course, the lower appellate Court, apart from other reasons, has found the, Plaintiffs purchase of the suit-lands to have been hit by Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act. 

10. The learned Advocate for the Petitioner has, however, alleged that the learned Additional District Judge-in-Charge was wrong in his finding on this point. On scrutiny, I find that the suit was instituted on 6.11.80 and the alleged purchase took place on 6.8.80. So, it is found that the suit was instituted later on, after the alleged purchase of the Plaintiff. Hence, it cannot be held that the purchase was hit by Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act. Mr. Akram Hossain Amin, the learned Advocate for the Opposite Parties, also concedes to this, but maintains that even if this question of application of SECTION 52 of the Transfer of Property Act is let out in the instant case, still it would be found that the Courts below, having carefully considered the materials on record, have concurrently and rightly found that the alleged Heba-bil-Ewaz is false and fraudulent and the same has not been acted upon and hence the basis of the claim of the Plaintiffs title and possession over the said .35 acre of land is lost. As to the other point canvassed by the learned advocate for the petitioner that even if the Plaintiff is not found in possession of any portion of the suit land, still he is entitled to a decree for partition. In reply to this contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner, Mr. Akram Hossain Amin, the learned Advocate for the Opposite Parties, has submitted that so far the Plaintiffs claim of title over the .35 acre of land has been proved to be false and baseless. Now remains his only claim of title for .08 acre of land allegedly acquired from one Sekander Ali, who is also Defendant No. 33 in this suit and who has been examined as D.W.2 on behalf of the Defendants, but he has stated in his deposition that the Plaintiff obtained a Kabala from him though he was not in possession in any portion of the suit land. He could not say in his evidence as to the identity of the land to which the said Kabala relates and further he has admitted that he was not in possession of the suit land and even he did not visit the suit land any time. Further, it appears that the Plaintiff has not also produced any witness in this connection to prove his purchase of the said .08 acre of land from Sekandar, possibly for the reason that it was a suit for partition only and not for declaration of title. The trial Court, of course, vaguely observed that the Plaintiff has title in .08 acre of land, but he has no possession over the same. The lower appellate Court did not, however, accept the said observation of the trial Court, rather doubted the genuineness of the Plaintiffs claim of title even over the .08 acre of the suit land also. 

11. It is, therefore, contended by the learned Advocate for the Opposite Parties that in any view of the matter, the Plaintiff cannot get any decree for partition in this suit, even for his alleged claim of .08 acre of land over which Plaintiffs right, title and interest has yet to be clearly decided and established. The learned Advocate for the Opposite Parties further submits that the Plaintiff, if so advised, may, however, seek his relief by way of filing an independent suit for declaration of his right and title over the said .08 acre of land with a prayer for recovery of possession or confirmation of possession, if found to be in possession, on payment of advalorem Court-fees. I have considered the above submissions of the learned Advocates of both the sides with regard to this .08 acre of land in suit and I find much force in the submission of the learned Advocate for the Opposite Parties and hold that in the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record and the position of law, the Plaintiff is not entitled to a decree for partition of this remaining .08 acre of land in the suit also. Having considered all aspects of the matter vis-a-vis the evidence on record, I find no illegality in the impugned judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court affirming those of the trial court and the same do not call for any interference by this court in revision. 

12. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. It appears that Mr. Akram Hossain Amin, the learned Advocate on behalf of the Opposite Parties has put in a counter affidavit in connection with this Rule with copy to the other side after conclusion of its hearing, but awaiting judgment. The same is however kept with the record. 

13. Let the lower Court's records along with a copy of this judgment be sent down expeditiously. 

End.

lawyer:
P. K. Bose, Advocate ------ for Appellant
Jamiruddin Sircar with Mir Hashtmat Ali, Advocates ------ For Respondent
parties:
Md. Shahidul Alam Khan & Others
Vs.
Md. Gulzar Alam & Others
full_judgment:
S. M. Husain J.—This Second Appeal arises out of a judgment of reversal in a suit for partition. The trial court dismissed the suit whereas the lower appellate court decreed the same against which the defendants have preferred this Second Appeal.

2. There is no dispute over the joint title and possession between the plaintiffs and the defendants with regard to the suit property. The defendant’s main objection was that all the properties jointly belonging to the plaintiffs and the defendants were not included in the hotch-potch of the Partition Suit and consequently there could not be any partial partition. The trial court dismissed the-suit on the ground that there could not be any partial partition between the parties whereas the lower appellate court decreed the suit holding that partial partition could be allowed on ground of equity and convenience where parties are not otherwise prejudiced by such partial partition. This finding of the lower appellate court has been challenged before this court in this Second Appeal.

3. At the outset it must be observed that before dismissing the suit on the ground of partial partition the trial court ought to have afforded an opportunity to both the plaintiffs and defendants to include those properties that were allegedly left out within the hotchpotch of the suit property by way of an amendment of the schedule to the plaint. The defendants while objecting to the plaintiffs prayer for partial partition ought to have applied before the trial court for inclusion of such properties which were left out of the hotchpotch because in any partition suit both the plaintiffs and the defendants stand in the same position with same right to claim share in the entire hotchpotch of the properties jointly held by the plaintiffs and the defendants. In any view of the matter without enabling the parties to include all the properties jointly held by the plaintiffs and the defendants within the hotchpotch of the partition suit, the trial court wrongly dismissed such suit.

4. The question now raised is whether the lower appellate court rightly decreed the suit when admittedly all the properties belonging to the plaintiffs and the defendants were not included in the hotchpotch of the partition suit. It appears that while the defendants obeying the non-inclusion of the joint properties referred to Khatian Number 25, 72 and 33. So far as Khatian No. 72 and 33 are concerned admittedly there was no community of interest between the plaintiffs and the defendants in the properties covered in such Khatians as have been found by both the courts below concurrently and consequently there was no cause for inclusion of any property covered by Khatian NO. 72 and 33 in the hotchpotch of the present partition suit which is now exclusively concerned with the khatian number 25 only.

5. So far as Khatian No. 25 is concerned it includes more than about 54 plots of lands out of which the plaintiffs have claimed partition with regard to six plots of lands only. For the rest of about 48 plots of lands not included in the hotchpotch of the partition suit, the plaintiffs alleged that these plots were already separately held between the plaintiffs and the defendants by virtue of a Deed of Gift executed and registered on 5.8.1933 at Jalpaigury now Within the State of West Bengal in India. The original copy, the registered deed of gift was allegedly and evidently lying with the defendant No. 1 as guardian of plaintiffs who were minors at the relevant time. A certified copy of the registered deed of gift issued by the Sub-Registrar of Jalpaigury was produced in court and attesting witnesses were examined in court in support of such deed- of gift. The certified copy of the Deed of Gift issued by the Sub-Registrar of Jalpaiguri in India was not however formally admitted in evidence because being a forged document it was not attested by any authority of the Government in the then East Pakistan. So far this registered deed of gift is concerned, it included all the plots of lands covered by Khatian No. 25 and it also allotted different plots of lands between the plaintiffs and defendants specifically while delivering the possession of such plots of lands to the plaintiffs and the defendants. The deed of gift however omitted specifically to allot six plots of lands within Khatian No. 25 between the plaintiffs and the defendants and these omissions in the deed of gift caused the plaintiffs to institute the present partition suit for the allocation of the remaining six plots of lands in Khatian No. 25 between the plaintiffs and the defendants.

6. From the foregoing facts and circumstances of the case it, would clearly appear that it is an admitted fact and concurrently held by both the courts below that the plaintiffs and the defendants were separately, possessing all the plots of lands covered by khatian: No. 25 excepting the present six plots of lands by virtue of the deed of gift registered and executed Jalpaiguri on 5.8.33. That apart from the remaining six plots of lands in khatian. No. 25, all other plots of lands were held by the plaintiffs and the defendants separately as mentioned in the registered deed of gift when admittedly the plaintiffs and defendants were possessing their respective plots of lands separately excepting the present six plots of lands within khatian No. 25. There was no occasion for either the plaintiffs or the defendants to cause any partition of such plots of lands which were held and possessed separately by the plaintiffs and the defendants. The present cause of action for instituting the present partition suit arose be-cause six plots of lands within khatian No. 25 were not allotted separately to the plaintiffs and the defendants. In such circumstances the question is whether, it. could be called a partial partition if at all, and if so; whether such partial partition could be allowed in the present facts and circumstances of the case for ends of justice and equity.

<u>7. When, admittedly the plaintiffs and the defendants were holding all other plots of lands exempting six plots of lands in khatian No. 25, it must be presumed that there was an amicabla partition between the parties by virtue of the registered deed of gift. Since six plots of Iands in Khatian No. 25 were not specifically allotted to the plaintiff and the defendants in the registered deed of gift the parties had to hold and possess such lands jointly by compulsion. The general rule is that a suit for partition shall include the entire properties of the co-sharers held and possessed jointly but in the present case it cannot be said that all the plots of lands in khatian No. 25 were held and possessed jointly by the plaintiffs and the defendants since excepting six plots of lands and all other plots of lands were held and possessed by the plaintiffs and the defendants separately. Only with regard to six plots of lands the plaintiffs and the defendants are holding and possessing such properties jointly as, co-sharers. It must be observed that the general rule to include the entire properties of all the co-sharers held and possessed jointly in a suit for partition is a rule of equity and which could be relaxed when a partition might be necessary for ends of justice and without causing any prejudice to any party. A rule of equity as opposed to a rule of law shall be applied on the convenience of the parties concerned and may be relaxed from time to time for ends of justice in the interest of the parties concerned without causing prejudice to anyone. This view was taken by Mr. Justice Ibrahim in a decision reported in 5 D.L.R. at page 511. In the present case when evidently there is no occasion to include all the plots of lands covered by Khatian No. 25 within the hotchpotch of the partition suit since excepting the present disputed six plots of lands all other plots of lands were held and possessed by the plaintiffs and the defendants separately, there was valid reason for the plaintiffs to sue for partition only with regard to six plots of lands admittedly held and possessed jointly by the plaintiff and the defendants.</u>

8. In the foregoing facts and circumstances of the case stated hereinbefore, the lower appellate court rightly decreed the plaintiff’s suit for partition against the defendants with regard to six plots of lands in khatian No. 25 between the plaintiffs and the defendants. There is no illegality in the judgment and of the lower appellant’s court and consequently this appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
M.H. Khondker, Sr. Advocate, instructed by Sharifuddin Chaklader, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Appellants
Md. Yasin, Advocate, instructed by Md. Nowab Ali, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the respondent
parties:
Jonab Ali Sardar & Ors.
Vs.
Taser Ali Fakir & Another
full_judgment:
Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J.:- This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment and order in Letters Patent No. 7 of 1967.

2. Plaintiffs' case in short was that the suit land i.e. 1/3rd of C.S. plot No. 839. 832. 842, 867 and 869 and half of C.S. plot No. 797 and whole of other plots appertaining to jama of Rs. 7/- belonged to Ichhamoyee Dashi who sold the same to Abdul Mannan an and pro forma defendant No.6 by kabala dated 28-2-36 in equal shares. Abdul Mannan sold his entire interest i.e. -/8/- annas share of the jama to the plaintiff by kabala dated 7-9-57 pro forma defendant No. 6 Jabed Mondal also sold some portion of the share of the jama to the plaintiff. The plaintiff and pro forma defendant No. 6 were threatened with dispossession and as such they filed Title Suit No. 205 of 1958 The suit ended in compromise by the said compromise decree. The plaintiff and pro forma defendant No.6 got 1/3rd share of the suit dag i.e. the suit land. The defendants 1 to 5 who were pro forma defendants Nos.30 to 34 in that suit got the remaining portion of the suit plot. Thereafter pro forma defendant No.6 sold his remaining share in the plot to the plaintiff and the plaintiff became owner of 16 annas share of the suit land and since then he was in possession of the same asserting his own right. In the recent rent roll plaintiffs name was not correctly recorded and being encouraged by the finding of a case under section 19(1) and 19(2) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the defendants threatened the plaintiff with dispossession from the suit land. Hence the suit.

3. The defendants 1 to 5 contended inter alia, that in terms of solenama filed in Title Suit No. 205 of 1958 plaintiff got 13rd share of the suit land of that suit except plot No. 797 in which the plaintiff got half share. The remaining portions of the suit land of that suit in the allotment of the defendants and as such according to the defendants, the plaintiff was not entitled to get any relief whatsoever in the suit.

4. The trial court came to the conclusion that on the interpretation of the Solenama Ext. 2 plaintiff was entitled to 1/3rd of the suit dag and not of the suit land. In that view of the matter plaintiff's suit was decreed.

5. The appellate court below concurred with the findings of the trial court and dismissed the appeal preferred by defendants No 1 to 5.

6. In Second Appeal being S. A. No. 619 of 1962 the learned Single Judge allowed the appeal and set aside the judgments and decrees of the Courts below and decreed the suit in part holding that a decree be passed in favour of the plaintiff for 1/3rd of the land of the plots 832, 839, 842. 867, 869 and half of the C.S. plot No. 797 in respect of the quantum of land which were the subject matter of the suit No. 205 of 1958.

7. Leave was granted for filing a Letters Patent Appeal and the High Court Division in Letter Patent Appeal came to the conclusion that crucial point of interpretation of Ext. 2 Solenama Learned Judges considered the Solenama Ext.2 and concluded that the compromise was effected with regard to the land of the decree and not with regard to the land in suit. In Letters Patent Appeal it was noticed that the trial court and the appellate Court below correctly construed the Solenama that in that compromise the entire land of dags were divided into 1 3rd  and 2/3rd between the parties and the plaintiff will get 1/3rd and defendant will get 2 3rd of the dags in the suit. The learned Single Judge on the other hand held that the Solenama mentioned the expression ‘নালিশী জমি’ which means the lands were subject matte of the suit and whole of the dags were not the subject matter of the suit. In Letters Patent Appeal it was obscene:

“Though the whole dags were not the subject matter of the suit the plaintiff claimed in that suit by compromise the said dags were divided among the parties which was quite legal and it cannot be said that only the lands of the suit were divided.

It was also noticed that the parties in the previous suit and the present suit were the same and in that context it was viewed that the entire dag was subject matter of the compromise. The learned Judges pointedly mentioned: "It is compromised between the parties claiming title to the suit dags and in that compromise the whole dags have been divided between the parties". It was further found that the compromise was given effect to by the Court. In this view of the matter the judgment and order of the learned Single Judge in Second Appeal was set aside and those of the trial court and the first appellate court were restored.

8. Leave was granted to consider the legal effect of Ext.2 Solenama.

<u>9. Mr. M.H. Khondker appearing for the defendants appellants contended that Ext.2 did not divide the whole dags and even if it had purported to be done it was inadmissible in evidence not being registered as it compromised property outside suit inasmuch as such solenama is compulsorily registerable under section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act. The entire document has been placed before us and on reading of the Solenama we are of the view that the High Court Division in Letters Patent had correctly interoperated the document and rightly restored those of the trial and the lower appellate Court below. The expression ‘নালিশী জমি’ created the confusion but reading the solenama as a whole there is no doubt that the entire dags of the parties were divided as per the terms of the compromise. The interpretation of the Ext.2 is concluded by the concurrent findings of the facts of the courts below and the learned Single Judge in Second Appeal ought not to have disturbed those findings only on the assuming meaning of expression namely ‘নালিশী জমি’ which has now paved the way for controversy. The contention grounded on the admissibility of the document has no force. Section 17, no doubt, postulates that certain document must be registered but sub-section (2) provides that nothing in clause (b) and (c) of sub-section (1) applies to any decree or order of a court (except a decree or order ex pressed to be made on a compromise and comprising immovable property other than that which is the subject matter of the suit or proceeding). Clause 6 was amended in 1929 following a decision of Privy Council in Hemendra Kumari V. Midnapur Zamindary, A.I.R. 1919 P.C. 79. After the amendment the position appears to be this: If the case of compromise relates to property which is not the subject matter of the suit or proceeding then obviously latter part of Clause 6 would take away the exception and to such a case clause (b) or (c) as the case may be would apply and such a document would be liable for registration. Where the compromise deals only with the properties in suit and the Court passes a decree in accordance therewith such a case will fall within the exception and such a decree would not require registration. The words "and not being decree and order: in section 50 obviously refer to decrees and orders which are exempted from registration under the amended section 17(2) (vi). It is a question of fact whether the compromise has been acted upon or is covered by a decree which is a mixed question. If the compromise has been acted upon or is covered by decree then it is settled law that compromise is exempt from registration.</u>

10. Mr. Khondker could not assail the point that the compromise had been acted upon. Solenama was given effect to and construction of the solenama by the two courts below clearly shows that the entire dags were subject matter of the compromise. Therefore clause 6 covers the case and the document exempt from registration. The argument build on sub-section (1) of section 17 does not stand.

In the result this appeal is dismissed No costs.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition For Leave To Appeal No. 576 of 1994
lawyer:
Mr. A.B.M. Nurul Islam, Senior Advocate instructed by Mr. Md. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Petitioners. 
Mr. Md. Nawab Ali, Advocate-on ----- For Respondent No. 1. 
Respondent No.2: Not represented.
parties:
Asia Khatun being dead her legal heirs and representatives Bulbul Ahmed and others ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Rahatun Nesa and another ----- Defendant—Respondents
full_judgment:
Latifur Rahman, J: Plaintiff- petitioner filed an application before the Sub ordinance Judge, Chandpur in Title Suit No. 85 of 1990 for staying all further proceedings of Title Execution Case No. 6 of 1985, arising out of a suit for partition, being Partition Suit No. 53 of 1958. The trial Judge rejected this application by his order dated 17.2.91. This order was unsuccessfully challenged before the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 949 of 1991. Plaintiff- petitioner now seeking leave to appeal from the impugned judgment of the High Court Division.

2. One Yeasin Bhuiya son of late Mondir Mahmud filed Partition Suit No. 53 of 1958 and the same was decreed in preliminary form on 23.5.59 and the final decree was passed on 24.9.85. Thereafter Title Execution Case No. 6 of 1985 was started for exaction of the final decree. After passing of the final decree in that partition suit one Asia Khatoon filed Title Suit No. 153 of 1985 for a declaration that the decree passed in the partition suit's void, illegal and not binding on her and for setting aside the judgment and decree of that partition suit. In that suit Asia Khatoon prayed for staying the further proceeding of Title Execution Case No. 6 of 1985 and stay was granted. After the disposal of the aforesaid suit, the stay of Title Execution Case No. 6 of 1985 was vacated. Asia Khatoon being old her son in law Md. Adbul Momen, her constituted attorney filed Tide Suit No. 85 of 1990 for a declaration that the solenama that was Filed on 25.10.90 in Title Suit No. 153 of 1985 was illegal, void and collusive and for setting aside the dismissal order. Asia Khatuns Attorney also prayed for stay of the proceeding of Title Execution Case No. 6 of 1985 and the same was rejected. Subsequently, the High Court Division affirmed the order of rejection of the Subordinate Judge; Chandpur.

3. Mr. A. B. M Nurul Islam, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that all necessary parties were not impleaded in the partition suit and more particularly Asia khatun was a necessary party who was not made a party in the partition suit.

<u>4. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division found that admittedly the suit property originally belonged to one Mandir Mahmud and that all his successors were made parties in the partition suit including the husband of Asia Khatoon, Md. Ibrahim son of Soleman one of the daughters of Mandir Mahmud. The learned Single Judge correctly held that Asia Khatun being the wife of Md. Ibrahim was not at all a co-sharer in the suit land and consequently she was not a necessary party in the partition suit. Further, it appears that Asia Khatun filed successive suits to frustrate the decree obtained in Partition Suit No.53 of 1958. The learned Single Judge correctly found that the approach of the present plaintiff in staying further proceeding of Title Execution Case No. 6 of 1985 was not bonafide. Whether the execution case should be stayed or not is purely a matter of judicial discretion for the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division. Proper discretion having been exercised on the materials on record, the same calls for no interference.</u>

5. The petition is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Md. Latifur Rahman, with Mr. Harun-ur-Rashi Mrs. Sultana R. Nahar, Advocates ----- for the appellant. 
Mr. Mvi. Md. Wahidullah with Mr. Md. Aminul Islam Mondal, Advocates ----- for the respondents.
parties:
Lalu Uddin ----- Appellant
Vs.
Hemayet Hossain and others ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
Muhammad Ansar Ali, J: This Second Appeal at the instance of the plaintiff a is Directed against the judgment and decree dated 16 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Khulna in Title Appeal No. 192/75 allowing the appeal and reversing those dated 28.2.75 of the learned Munsif, 2nd Court, Khulna passed in Title Suit No. 300 of 1969 for specific performance of a contract.

2. The plaintiffs case in brief is that the original defendant no.1 Sarat Chandra Sarkar contracted to sell the suit land to the plaintiff and to that, effect, he executed a deed of contract an the 20th Bhadra, 1370, B. S. containing the certain terms; that a sum of Tk. 2500/- was fixed as the consideration for the sale of land out of which Taka 2,000/- was paid to the defendant in advance and the plaintiff the reafter was put into possession of the suit land that if Sarat could refund the earnest money of Tk. 2,000/- to the plaintiff by Aswin 1373 B.S. then the plaintiff would return the deed of contract and give back the possession of the suit land to the original defendant No.1 Sarat and if by that date Tk. 2,000/-was not refunded, the defdt no. 1 would receive the rest amount of Tk. 500/- and execute a deed of transfer for the suit land in favour of the plaintiff, failing which the plaintiff would be at liberty to get the deed of transfer executed and registered in his favour in respect of the suit-land through court in which case the unpaid amount of Tk. 500/- would he treated as costs for the registration of the Kabala deed; that the original defendant Sarat neither refunded the earnest money nor executed any Kabala deed in favour of the plaintiff by Aswin, 1373 B. S. or thereafter in spite of the plaintiff's repeat requests; that the original defendant No. 1 went on making delay on this or the plea, s the plea of obtaining permission from the Government for registration of the Kabala etc. in view the Disturbed Persons Rehabitations  Ordinance, 1964 but although the said Ordinance was repealed in favour of the plaintiff. Hence the suit.

3. The defendant No. 1 (kha) a substituted heir of defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 2, an added defendant contested the suit by filing two separate written statements almost on the same grounds inter-alia that the plaintiff had no cause of action; that the suit was bad for defect of parties; that the suit was barred by limitation and also by the principles of estoppel, waiver and acquisence. The defendants denied that there was any bainapatra (deed of contract) executed by Sarat Chandra Sarkar in favour of the plaintiff for sale of the suit-land or that the plaintiff paid in advance to the defendant a sum of Tk. 2,000/- as earnest money out of the total consideration. The defendants stated that the real facts were that Sarat Chandra Sarkar did not at all enter into any contract for sale of his land with the plaintiff. The defendant No. 1 (kha) stated that Sarat Chandra defendant No. 1 sold out only 5 bighas of his land from the suit-joma to the plaintiff who got executed by said Sarat Kumar a blank stamp-paper to be made a borga Kabuliyat but the plaintiff fraudulently made the same a bainapatra (deed of contract) for sale of the suit-land. The defendant No. 2 stated that he purchased the suit-land from Sarat by registered kabala deed dated 4.7.69 and since then he was possessing the same He further stated that he was not sware of the alleged bainapatra (deed of contract).

4. The learned Munsif framed the following issues for determination in the suit:

1. Is the suit maintainable in its present form?

2. Is the story of the alleged contract true?

3. Is the plaintiff entitiled to get a decree for specific performance of contract on the of the alleged bainapatra?

4. To what relief, if any, is the plaintiff entitled?

5. The plaintiff examined 5 P.Ws. and the contesting defendant examined 4 D.Ws. in support of their respective cases.

6. The learned Munsif heard the learned Advocates of both the sides and altimately on consideration of the evidences and other materials on record, found the deed of contract Ext. 1 to be genuine, valid and duly executed by defendant No. 1 Sarat Chandra Sarkar in favour of the plaintiff and came to the finding that the plaintiff was entitled to get a decree for specific performance of contract on the basis of the said deed of contract (bainapatra ) Ext. 1 and accordingly decreed the suit on contest as against the defendant No. 1 (Kha) substituted heir of deceased defendant No. 1 and the added defendant No. 2 with costs and exparte against the rest without cost by his judgment and decree dated 28.2.75.

7. Being aggrieved by the same, none but the added contesting defendant No. 2 Hemayet Hossain only preferred an appeal being Title Appeal No. 192 of 1975 in the court of the learned District Judge, Khulna and the same was subsequently heard by the learned Subordinate Judge, Khulna on transfer. He formulated the only point for determination to the effect as to whether the plaintiff was entitled to get the decree sought for.

8. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the materials on record, disbelieved the plaintiffs case and found that the contract (Ekrarnama) Ext. 1 was not a genuine one and hence reversed the finding of the trial court. As regards possession, he came to a finding that the plaintiff could not prove his possession in the suit-land. He further observed that the plaintiff failed to discharge the onus cast upon him in proving the factum of the deed of contract as well as the possession in the suit-land. In that view of the matter, it was held that the plaintiff was not entitled to the decree for specific performance of contract as prayed for and the appeal was allowed and the decision of the trial court was reversed with the dismissal of the suit.

9. The plaintiff being aggrieved by the aforesaid decision dated 16.4.77 of the learned Subordinate Judge preferred this second appeal in this court.

10. Mr. Md. Latifur Rahman with Mr. Harun-ar-Rashid, the learned Advocates appeared for the plaintiff-appellant and Mr. Md. Wahidullah with Mr. Aminul Islam, the learned Advocates appeared for the defetidnat respondent Nos. 2,1 (ka) Debola Rani Sarkar and 4(gha) Sarala Bala Desi. It appears from the records that notice of this appeal was duly served upon all the defendant -respondents, but none appeared on behalf of the contesting defendant- respondent no. 1 Hemayet Hossain and respondent No.3 (Kha) Kusum Rani Sarkar. The aforesaid learned Advocates appeared only on behalf of the defendant-respondent Nos. 2, 1 (Ka) and 4 (Cha) along with others who were substituted on the death of the contesting defendant No. 1 Sarat Chandra Sarkar in the court of below but did not contest the suit which was decreed ex-parte against them by the trial court. It is only the present respondent No.1 and respondent No.3 (Kha) who contested the suit and being aggrieved by the decision of the trial court, it is only the present respondent No. 1 Hemayet Hossain who preferred an appeal being Title Appeal No. 102/1975 in the court of the District Judge, Khulna which was on transfer heard and disposed of by the learned Subordinate Judge, Khulna reversing the decision of the trial court by the impugned judgment and decree.

11. Mr. Latifur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff- appellant placed before me both the judgments and decrees of the courts below and then pointed out, firstly that the respondents No. 2, 1 (Ka) and 4 (Gha) have no locus standi to contest this appeal. The judgment and decree of the trial court stand binding on them as they did not prefer any appeal against the same before the court of appeal below. So far as respondent No. 3 (Kha) Kusum Rani Sarkar, wife of late Sarat Chandra Sarkar is concerned, it is pointed out that she contested the suit in the trial court but the same was decreed in favour of the present plaintiff-appellant with cost against her as well as against the contesting defendant No. 2 i.e. the present respondent No.1 in this appeal, but as against that decision of the trial court, this respondent No.3 (kha) who was  defendant No.1 (Kha) in the trial court did not prefer any appeal and as such the decision of the trial court having not been challenged by her in appeal must have a binding effect on her and further at this stage in second appeal, also, there is no appearance by her through any advocate in this court. Now, defendant No. 2 the present respondent No.1, of course preferred an appeal as stated earlier in the lower appellate court which was allowed and the trial court's decision was reversed and the Suit was dismissed on contest with cost. Now, the said impugned judgment and decree of the court of appeal below is under challenge here in this appeal, but unfortunately in spite of due service of notice upon the said defendant-respondent No.1, no lawyer has been engaged or appeared to represent him and to contest this appeal.

12. Mr. Latifur Rahman, however challenged the aforesaid judgment and decree of the court of appeal below on merit contending inter-alia that the lower appellate court by mistaken assumption of facts of the case and through misreading and also non-consideration of the evidence on record, particularly the evidence with regard to the first payment of the earnest money for an amount of Tk. 500/- by the plaintiff to the defendant No.1, late Sarat Chandra Sarkar who of course admitted his signature on the said document i.e. the deed of contract (Ekrarnama) Ext. 1, but denied the contents incorporated therein and contended that his signature was obtained not for making the deed of contract for sale of the suit-land, but for making a borga-kabuliyat for cultivation of the suit-land under the plaintiff, arrived at erroneous conclusion. He further submitted that the trial court carefully examined the genuineness of the said deed of contract, Ext. 1 as per the issues framed in the suit and considered the evidence on record as to the execution and the contents of the said document and rightly found the same to be fully genuine and decreed the suit which ought to have been upheld by the court of appeal below.

13. I have already stated above that the plaintiff in order to prove his case examined 5 P. Ws. and the contesting defendants examined 4 D. Ws. in support of their respective cases. P. W. 1 is the plaintiff himself. It is in his evidence that he earlier paid Taka 500/- to the defendant No. 1 Sarat Chandra Sarkar a few days before the execution of the deed of contract, Ext. l and thereafter at the time of actual execution of the same on the 28th Bhadra, 1370 B. S. he paid the rest amount of Tk. 1,500/- to the said executant defendant No.1 Sarat Chandra Sarkar, since deceased and he further stated that the total consideration was fixed at Tk. 2,500/- out of which he already paid up a sum of Tk. 2,000/- by two instalments as stated above and if the executant defendant No.1 Sarat Chandra Sarkar could return that money by Ashwin, 1375 B. S. and then he (Plaintiff) would have returned the deed of contract and also given up possession of the suit-land to him the defendant No.1 according to terms of contract but he i. e. Sarat Chandra Sarkar, the defendant No. 1 failed to do so. Now, in his cross-examination P.W. 1 could not be shaken on the above points in any way by the defendants. The plaintiff however brought Abul Hossain Haradar P. W. 3, the writer of the said deed of contract and also as a witness who categorically stated that he was a deed- writer of Rampal and he wrote the aforesaid deed of contract Ext. 1 under the instructions of defendant No.1 Sarat Chandra Sarkar. He of course stated that the payment of Tk. 1,500/- to the defendant No.1 was done in his presence, but it was also in the evidence of P. W. 1 that earlier the plaintiff paid Tk. 500/- to the defendant No. 1 Sarat Chandra Sarkar before the subsequent payment to Tk. 1,500/-. About the earlier payment of Tk. 500/- to the defendant No. 1, P. W. 4 Sheikh Arman also stated in his deposition. Of course, the sum of Tk. 1,500/-was paid in his presence to the executant Sarat Chandra Sarkar before the execution of the said deed of contract Ext. 1. A suggestion from the said of the contesting defendant was given to the above P.Ws. to the effect that the said document of contract was anti dated and meant for borga kabuliyat only, was totally denied by both of them, P. W. 3 was an attesting witness of the said deed of contract. He came to prove the execution of the said deed Ext.1 in his presence. Against these witnesses it appears that no enmity or grudge was suggested by defendant No.1.

I therefore find nothing to disbelieve them P.W. 5 Siddique was a laborer who used to work under the plaintiff to cultivate the land. He stated that it was not a fact that Jamshed was not in possession in the suit-land. He was a witness on behalf of the plaintiff to prove plaintiff's possession. Again P.W. 2 one Haripada, claimed to be a witness of possession of the plaintiff in the suit-land but in cross-examination, he stated that he could not say how much land the plaintiff possessed. On the other hand D.W.1 defendant 1 (Kha) wife of late Sarat Chandra Sarkar defendant No. 1 stated in her cross-examination that it was not a fact that Aroz Ali did not possess the suit-land. She of course stated in her cross-examination by defendant No. 2 that is was not a fact that her husband in collusion with Araj Ali made a bainapatra in favour of the plaintiff. She of course pleaded her ignorance about the deed of contract Ext. 1 entered into by the plaintiff and her deceased husband D. W. 2 Atul Krishna was also a witness of defendant's possession P. W. 3 Araj Ali Sheikh, father of his minor son Hemayet Hossain, defendant No. 2 claimed to have purchased 2.33 acres of land from the suit-jama from defendant No. 1 late Sarat Chandra Sarkar in the name of her said minor so. He also pleaded ignorance of the deed of contract Ext. 1. He further stated that he came to know about the same in the 1st part of July, 1969. In cross-examination, he stated that the suit-land was about 3 miles away from his house. He also stated that he purchased the suit-land on 4.7.69 by registered kabala deed Ext. A (1) and that the area of the suit land was 2.33 acres which he was possessing after purchase. He further stated that he was not aware of any bainapatra between plaintiff and the deceased defendant no. 1. In his cross-examination, by the plaintiff, he however expressed his readiness to receive the consideration money of his purchased land, if paid back by the vendor and to recovery the suit-land.

14. Now, both the courts below disbelieved the evidence of possession on behalf of the plaintiff over the suit-land and relied on those of the D.Ws. and held that the plaintiff failed to prove his possession in the suit-land. The finding of possession arrived by both the courts below being a concurrent finding of fact, is binding on this court and it has nothing to in therefore with the same in second appeal.

15. But, it may be noticed that the finding as to the genuineness of the contract vide Ext. 1 is not concurrent. The lower appellate court has differed with the finding of the trial court and reversed the same. Now, the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant is that the finding and decision of the court of appeal below are not proper finding and decision of reversal.

<u>16. Let me see how far the contention of the learned Advocate is correct. From the analysis of the evidence on record, it appears that the learned Subordinate Judge failed to consider the material particulars of the evidence on behalf of the plaintiff to the effect that not only 1,500/- Taka, but also Taka 500/- more was paid earlier to the executant late Sarat Chandra Sarkar that means according to the contract, out of the total consideration of TK. 2500/-, the executant Late Sarat Chandra Sarkar defendant no. 1 received Tk. 2,000/- in all from he plaintiff and executed the deed of contract Ext. 1. The P. Ws. who had no enmity with the defendants categorically stated that on receipt of the consideration money of Tk. 2,000/- from the plaintiff, the defendant no. 1 Sarat Chandra Sarkar executed the bainapatra Ext. 1. i.e. deed of contract; but the lower appellate court through misconception and misreading of the evidence on record wrongly and arbitrarily disbelieved the story of payment of the said consideration money of Tk. 2,000/- to the executant Sarat Chandra Sarkar before the execution of the deed of contract in question and thereby committed serious illegality in deciding the genuineness of the deed of contract Ext. and as a result there has been a failure of justice. The finding of the lower appellate court reversing that of the trial court on question of genuineness of the deed of contract Ext. 1 is not at all a proer finding of reversal based on any sound reasoning and proper consideration of the evidence on record. The above finding of the lower appellate court appears have been arrived at due to non- consideration as well as misreading of the material piece of evidence. Hence, the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge as to the genuineness of the bainapatra Ext. I is wholly incorrectly and illegal. As such the decision based on such an illegal and arbitrary finding can not be sustained in law. However, it seems to me that the trial-court rightly found the deed of contract Ext. 1 as a genuine one for sale of the land in question of the defendant no.1 late Sarat Chandra Sarkar to the plaintiff and the contract vide Ext. 1 appears to have been duly entered into and genuinely executed by the vendor defendant no.1 on receipt of the earnest money as mentioned above. The trial court appears to have correctly found the same as a genuine and lawful one and accordingly decreed the suit for its enforcement through the specific performance of the contract as prayed for subject to the encumbrance created by Ext. A(1). The finding of the court of appeal below as to the genuineness and validity of the contract Ext. 1 does not appear to be a proper finding of reversal. Hence, the same is liable to be set aside in the interest of justice. In the instant case it is however interesting to note that on the death of the contesting defenant no.1 out of the substituted defendants only defendant 1(kha) and the added defendant no.2 contested the suit and the others did not, again as against the trial court's decree in favour of the plaintiff as against all the defendants, only the added defendant no.2, the present respondent No. 1 SK. Hemayet Hossain @ Ali preference the appeal and his case was that he purchased the suit-land from the defendant no.1 late Sarat Chandra Sarkar vide Ext. 4(1) dated 4.7.69 for a valuable consideration of Tk. 3,000/- without the knowledge of notice of the said deed of contract Ext. 1. Now, when except defendant No. 2, the other defendants had not challenged the decree of the trial court by preferring any appeal, the said decree stands binding on them and as to the gunuinenes of the deed of contract Ext. 1, the defendant no. 2, who claimed to have purchased the suit-land for valuable consideration without knowledge and notice of the contract, was not supposed to know or say anything about the execution and genuineness of the said deed of contract Ext. 1. However, it seems that the lower appellate court without proper application to his judicial mind to the evidence on record, in fact through mistaken assumption of facts and misreading and non-consideration of some material piece of evidence most illegally and arbitrarily held that the bainapatra i.e. deed of contract Ext. 1 was not a genuine one and on such finding reversed the decision of the trial court resulting in a serious miscarriage of justice. Now, in this court, the contesting defendant no.2 is the respondent no.1 but as has been stated above, on one has come to appear to represent him in this court in spite of due service of notice upon him and with regard to the other respondents, the Contesting defendant No.1 (kha) did neither prefer any appeal in the court of appeal below nor as respondent no. 3 (kha) did appear in this court to contest present appeal, though the suit was decreed against him also by the trial court. So far the other 2 respondent nos. 2, 1(ka) and 4(Gha) they did not either contest the suit or prefer aliy appeal against the trial courts decree, but now they have recently appointed M/S. Md. Wahidullah and another as their Advocates to contest the present second appeal and to question the legality of the trial court's decree, which is not permissible in law as they did not either contest the suit or file any appeal against the trial court's decree.</u>

17. Hence, at this stage they can be allowed to challenge the trial court's decision as respondents which is binding on them. Having regard to my above observations and findings, I am therefore of the view that the impugned judgment and decree of the court of appeal below are wholly bad and illegal and the same are liable to be set aside and those of the trial court, be upheld

18. In the result, this second appeal is allowed. The impugned judgment and decree of the court of appeal below are set aside and those of the learned Munsif are upheld and restored. There will be no order as to costs in this appeal in the facts and circumstances of the case. Let the lower court's records be sent down expeditiously.

End.

(From the Judgment and order dated 14.8.85 passed by the High Court Division, 
Dhaka, in Civil Revision No. 414 of 1983).
full_judgment:
Latifur Rahman, J.: This appeal by special leave at the instance of the plaintiff is directed against the judgment of the High Court Division, Dhaka, in Civil Revision No. 41 of 1983, reversing the appellate judgment in Title Appeal No. 245 of 1981.

2. The plaintiffs case in short, is that the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 101 of 1974 was fraudulent, void, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiff. The plaint case is that defendant No. 1 filed the aforesaid Title Suit No. 101 of 1974 against Amulya Prashad Ghose, husband of the present plaintiff and by suppressing the summons and notices of the said suit and by filing a forged, fraudulent and collusive solenama got compromise decree for specific performance of contract. Her further case is that her husband Amulya Prashad did not appear in the aforesaid suit and did not execute any solenama or any vokalatnama and the signatures on the solenama and vokalatnama are all forged and fabricated. Defendant No. 1 who was plaintiff in Title Suit No. 101 of 1974 contested the suit contending, inter alia, that the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 101 of 1974 is not fraudulent and void. The defendant's positive case is that, in that suit Amulya Prashad himself appeared and filed the solenama and the decree was passed after due service of sumons and no fraud was practised either upon the Court or upon the defendant of that suit.

3. The trial Judge dismissed the suit by holding that the solenama passed in the earlier  suit was a genuine one. On appeal, the lower appellate Court decreed the suit by holding that no summons were served upon the defendant of that suit and that the solenama was a forged and fabricated document. The High Court Division in revision set aside the appellate judgment and decree and dismissed the suit.

4. In this appeal, leave was granted to consider whether the High Court Division in revision was legally justified in setting aside the finding of the final Court of fact, when the appellate Court, on assessment of evidences on record, both oral and documentary, came to definite finding of fact which, in revision, was binding on the High Court Division.

5. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Counsel for the plaintiff, submits that Section 73 of the Evidence Act authorises the Court to compare the disputed signatures and the lower appellate Court having done so has not committed any illegality in arriving at a finding of fact which the High Court Division could not set aside in revision.

6. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed further submits that comparison of signatures is a perfect legal mode of proof of handwriting and the Revisional Court having itself not compared the signatures, acted illegally and erroneously in setting aside that finding of fact. The learned Advocate, while elaborating his argument, has also referred to the other material findings of fact of the lower appellate Court to which the High Court Division did not at all apply its mind in setting aside the appellate Judgment.

7. At the outset, it is to be stated that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division did not himself compare the signatures purported to be of Amulya Prashad on the vokalatnama and solenama of title Suit No. 101 of 1974 with the admitted signature of Amulya on the plaint of the present suit.

8. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division has, of course, elaborately dealt in his judgment with regard to the question of comparison of the disputed signatures or writings with the admitted writings as contemplated under Section 73 of the Evidence Act. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division, while considering the question as to the genuineness of the impugned solenama, on the basis of which the impugned decree was passed himself, of course, without comparing the disputed signatures held that such comparison is hazardous and not free from errors. We like to mention here that law prescribes for such comparison of signatures or writings. Further, whether this method is inconclusive or hazardous can only be opined in the fact of a case, provided the same is compared by the Court itself. Since, in the present case, the Single Judge of the High Court Division has not done so, his approach was totally illegal and erroneous.

9. Herein below we will refer to the findings of the lower appellate Court on the question of comparison of disputed signatures as found by the lower appellate Court. In the present case, the signatures were not sent to the hand-writing expert for opinion and as a matter of fact there was no material before any Court below to find that those are genuine signatures. The lower appellate Court compared the disputed signatures of Amulya Prasad in solenama, Exhibit B, and in vokalatnama, Exhibit C in the earlier suit with the admitted signature of the present plaint and found the same to be of different hands. Apart from this comparison, the lower appellate Court also considered the oral evidence on record to find out the genuineness of the alleged solenama. The lower appellate Court in this regard considered the testimony of the defendant's witnesses namely, D.Ws. 4 and 5 who were the clerks of the Advocates in the earlier suit. D.W.4 deposed that he wrote the solenama Exhibit B and D.W.5 deposed that he wrote the vokalatnama, Exhibit Court behalf of defendant No. 1 (Amulya Prashad) of Title Suit No. 101 of 1974. Both these witnesses in their cross-examination admitted that the parties did not sign the solenama in their presence but they signed the same in presence of their respective lawyers. The lawyers who conducted Title Suit No. 101 of 1974 were not also examined in this case. Defendant No. 1, SK. Ansaruddin, only deposed that Amulya signed the vokalatunama and the solenama in Title Suit No. 101 of 1974. D.W.1 being himself interested in the suit, the learned lower appellate Court thought it fit and proper not to believe the testimony of D.W.1. Thus apart from comparison of the disputed signatures, the appellate court on consideration of the oral evidence on record came to a finding of fact as to the genuineness of the solanama in the earlier suit. This being a pure finding of fact, the learned Single Judge committed an illegality in revision to set aside this finding.

10. It may be mentioned here that apart from the above finding, the lower appellate Court had also given other cogent reasons for setting aside the earlier decree to which the learned single Judge of the High Court Division was totally oblivious. The lower appellate Court found from perusal of the record that in the earlier suit there is nothing to show that summons and notices were served upon the defendant of that suit, but rather those were suppressed. It appears from the appellate Judgment that the learned Munsif did not rely on the service return of summons, that is why he ordered for issuing of fresh notices under a registered post and the appellate Court found from the record of that case that actually no notice was sent from the Court and neither the postal receipt, nor acknowledgement due was there in the records of the case and there was no endorsement in the order sheet that the registered post was actually sent. Further, the appellate Court found from the evidence of defendant himself of the present suit that notice under registered post was not sent in the earlier suit. Thus, the lower appellate Court found that there was suppression of summons and notices. The lower appellate Court further found on consideration of the Materials on record that the learned Munsif, in order to ascertain the truth of otherwise of the solenama, fixed the case on 20.3.1975 for hearing of the solenama but without ascertaining the truth of the solenama he passed the ex-parte decree on the basis of solenama. This is the most material finding of the lower appellate Court with regard to the suppression of the processes on the defendant of that suit and filing of a collusive and fraudulent solenama and obtaining of a compromise decree. This material finding with regard to the suppression of processes having been accepted by the learned single Judge of the High Court Division, the Judgment of the appellate Court ought not to have been set aside merely on the ground that the comparison of signatures by the Court of appeal below is wrong and hazadrous. Further, the lower appellate Court found from the materials on record that in Enemy Property Case No. XII-16/68-69 dated 15.3.76 the husband of the plaintiff filed a petition against leasing out of some lands to the present defendant as the land belonged to his two other brothers. In that proceeding, Amullya Prashad claimed that he was in possession of his own share and prayed for leasing out the shares of his two enemy brothers. In that preceding the present defendant Sk. Ansaruddin was a party and he did not assert that he had already purchased the share of Amulya or that he has got a "sole-decree" on 19.5.75. The appellate Court also found that this defendant wanted to suppress the existence of "sole-decree" to the A.D.C. or to anybody else before the filing of the present suit. Further, the Bainapatra which is the basis of the decree of the earlier suit was not taken into evidence at the time of disposal of that suit. During the trial of the present suit also the Bainapatra was not properly proved or taken into evidence as the scribe and the attesting witnesses of the Baniapatra were not examined. P.W.5 was examined as an attesting witness of the bainapatra but he denied to have attested the same. Hence, the lower appellate Court found that the decree holder of Title Suit No. 101 of 1974 got a decree by suppression of summons and by filing a collusive and fraudulent solenama.

<u>11. Thus, the learned Single Judge has also committed another illegality in setting aside the appellate judgment and decree without applying its judicial mind to other materials and vital findings arrived at by the lower appellate Court on consideration of relevant evidence on record. Consequently, the judgment of the High Court Division is set aside.</u>

12. The appeal is allowed with costs and the suit is decreed.

End.
