parties:
Amiruddin Mondal (Md) and others ------ Petitioners
Vs 
Md Ashraf Ali and others ------ Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued at the instance of the plaintiff-respondents petitioners calling upon the defendant opposite party Nos. 1(a) to 16(1) to show cause as to why the impugned Judgment and decree dated 30-5-2000 (decree signed on 4-6-2000) passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Kurigram in Other Class Appeal No. 94 of 1999 allowing the appeal and setting aside the Judgment and decree dated 5-8-1999 (decree signed on 9-8-1999) passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Rawmari, Kurigram in other Suit No. 56 of 1984 should not be set aside and or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The present petitioners as plaintiff filed other Suit No. 56 of 1984 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Rawmari, Kurigram praying for a declaratory decree that the judgment and ex parte decree dated 19-1-1976 passed by the learned Munsif, Karigram in Other Class Suit No. 1286 of 1973 is fraudulent, collusive and not binding upon the plaintiff.

3. The case of the plaintiffs-petitioners, in short, is that the property as shown in schedule 'Ka' to the plaint appertaining to CS Khatian No. 59 in the name of Moyan Mondal and others and total land of that khatian was 18.55 acres. Before publishing the CS khatian the above lands were in two separate jotes, one of Taka 27 and another of Taka 41 and 10 annas only. Suit Plot Nos. 931/939/755/956/496/497and other land (Binnalishi) Plot Nos. 500/502/932/933/937/938/940/943/944/942/948/949 /950/951/952/953 were in the jote of Taka 27 which were owned by Shatu Sheik and Taripulla Sheikh. The other land (Binnalishi) plot Nos. 996/997/998/999/1001/1002/ 1003/1004/1005/1006/1007/1008/1009/1010/1011/1012/1013/1014/509/510/511/512/ 513/514/515/516 were in the jote of Taka 40 and 10 annas which were owned by Moyan Mondal, Zahan Mondal, Cherag Mondal and Mokful Mondal each having 4 annas share. Mojam Mondal by amicable settlement got plot Nos. 997/1000/1002/1003/1005/1006/1007/1011/1012/511/512. Majam Mondal built homestead in plot No. 512 and has been possessing rest of the lands by cultivation. Shabu and Tarikullah sold lands of jote of Taka 27 to Sonaullah and Mojam Mondal on 30-4-1917 by a deed of sale and delivered possession to them. By amicable partition between Mojam Mondal and Sonaullah, Mojam got 4.17 acres of land in suit plot Nos. 931/939/955/956/496/497 and Sanaullah got other lands (Binnalishi) in plot Nos. 500/502/932/933/937/938/940/942/943/944/947/948/949/953. Thereafter, Mojam transferred the suit lands measuring 4.17 acres to the plaintiff-petitioner No. 1 Amiruddin Mondal and Noyan Ali Mondal, father of the petitioner No. 2 Abdul Hakim on 12th Kartick of 1344 BS by unregistered Amalnama. Noyan Ali died leaving behind one son plaintiff No. 2. In CS khatian No. 59 wrongly four annas share was recorded in the khatian. Instead of the above wrong record Mojam Mondal possessed his lands fully RS decreed was also published wrongly and Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973 was decreed collusively. The plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land. The plaintiffs came to know the matter of wrong record on 20th Jaishta of 1384 BS. It would cause irreparable loss to the plaintiffs. This causes cloud on their title and interest and hence the suit.

4. The defendant Nos. 1-5, 7-12, 19(ka-ta) contested the suit denying material allegations made in the plaint stating, inter alia, that the names of Majam and others were recorded in CS khatian No. 59. Majam Mondal died leaving 6 sons, 7 daughters and 2 wives. Ebadullah and Ekramullah, sons of Mojam Mondal, sold 33 decimals of land to Sekandar and others. Nekjan and Najjuri, daughters of late Bayatullah son of Majam sold their shares with other lands. Ebadullah sold 10 decimals, Fulzan sold 31 decimals, Dudh Bibi sold 31 decimals, Idrish son of late Anna Bibi daughter of Majam Mondal sold 62 decimals, Deljan daughter of Rupashi Bibi daughter of Najam sold 31 decimals to Abul Ashem and Abul Hossain Ekramullah sold 43 decimals to Ebad Mondal, Ebad Mondal and others names were not recorded in RS record, hence they filed Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973 before the Court of Munsif, Kurigram and the suit was decreed ex parte against present plaintiffs who were defendants. The defendants have been possessing the suit land in ejmali. The plaintiffs filed the suit after creating forged papers. The Government of Bangladesh as the defendant No. 41 filed written statement but did not contest the suit. The learned Assistant Judge, Rawmari, Kurigram by his judgment and decree dated 5-8-1999 decreed the suit and declared the plaintiff's title in the suit land and also declared that ex parte decree passed in Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973 is null and void. Against the said judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Rawmari the defendants-opposite-parties preferred an appeal being Other Appeal No. 94 of 1999 before the learned District Judge, Kurigram. The learned Additional District Judge, by the impugned judgment and decree dated 30-5-2000 allowed the appeal upon setting aside the aforesaid judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge.

5. Being aggrieved by the impugned judgment and decree dated 30-5-2000 passed by the learned Additional District Judge the plaintiffs-respondents-petitioners preferred the revisional application and obtained the present Rule.

6. Mr Md Khalilur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitions, submits that the learned Additional District Judge committed an error of law in passing the impugned judgment and decree allowing the appeal and setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge in Other Suit No. 56 of 1984 without considering the material evidence on record. He then submits that the impugned judgment and decree passed by the Court of appeal below are bad in law, the findings arrived at by the Court of appeal below were based on misconceived view of fact and law which has resulted in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. He then submits that the trial Court on consideration of the evidence of both the parties rightly decreed the suit but the Court of appeal below on misconception of law and fact allowed the appeal upon setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court without reversing the findings of the trial Court to the effect that summons and notices were not duly served upon the present petitioners who were defendants in Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973 and this has resulted in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree should be set aside. He, finally, submits that the Court of appeal below considered the 2 registered amalnamas marked Exhibit 4(Ka) and 2 rent receipts marking out of the 3rd case which was not at all alleged by the defendant-opposite-parties and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set aside and the Rule should be made absolute. Mr Khalilure Rahman, the learned Advocate for the petitioner in support of his contention has referred to the judgment of the trial Court and submits that learned Assistant Judge having perused the case record of Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973 found that there was no recording of the service of summons upon the defendants who are the plaintiff in the present case and thereby rightly decreed the suit and setting aside the ex parte decree passed in Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973. In support of his contention he has cited the decisions in the cases of Md Abu Jabar Mia vs Abdul Motaleb and another reported in 5 MLR 249, Alauddin Khan vs Mohammad Sheikh & others reported in 2 MLR 383 and Government of Bangladesh and another vs Mashirur Rahman and others reported in 50 DLR (AD) 205 and submits that an ex parte decree may he set aside on 2 grounds namely, non-service of summons upon the defendants or the defendants were prevented by sufficient cause when the suit was taken upon for hearing.

7. Mr Md Abdul FIaque, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party, submits that there is no illegality in the impugned judgment and decree passed by the Court of appeal below in allowing the appeal and setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge as the plaintiffs-petitioners miserably failed to prove the title and possession of the suit land. He then submits that the Court of appeal below rightly found that the alleged amalnama and rent receipts are fraudulent and collusive documents which cannot create valid title in favour of the plaintiff and, as such, no illegality has been committed which does not require any interference by this Court and the Rule should be discharged. He further submits that the witnesses of the defendants and some of the witnesses of the plaintiffs proved the possession of the plaintiffs and the defendants in some portion of the suit land and that the plaintiffs failed to prove their title and possession on the entire suit land, the Court of appeal below rightly held that there was no need to set aside the ex parte decree passed in Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973 and, as such, the Rule should be discharged.

8. I have perused the revisional application, judgments and decrees passed by the Courts below, evidences of the witnesses and other materials on record.

9. In the instant case, the plaintiff No. 2 Md Hamid as PW 1 in examination-in-chief adduced evidence in support of his plaint case and also stated that the suit land originally belonged to Taripulla and Shabu Sheikh who before CS operation had sold out 13.50 bighas in favour of Sonaullah and Majam Mondal by registered deed in 1344 BS though Majam's name was recorded in the CS khatian along with other co-sharers but his share should have been 8 annas. Majam while in possession of the suit land by virtue of right and title transferred 4.17 acres of land by unregistered amalnama in favour of Amiruddin and Nayan on 12th Kartick, 1344 BS and delivered possession to them. The plaintiff No. 1 Amiruddin and the plaintiff No. 2 Md Abdul Hakim as the son of Nayan have been possessing the suit land but the present defendants as the plaintiffs collusively and secretly filed Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973 against the plaintiffs and obtained ex parte decree without serving notice upon the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs for the first time came to know about the ex parte decree passed in Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973 and the wrong recording of RS khatian on 20th Jaistha 1384 BS and hence the plaintiffs filed the suit for declaration of title in the suit land and also declared that the ex parte decree dated 19-11-1976 passed in Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973 is null and void. The plaintiffs also proved CS khatian No. 597247 and 49 which were marked as Exhibit 1 series. He also proved the certified copy of the registered deed dated 30-4-1970 which was marked as Exhibit 2 and the Government rent receipts marked as Exhibit 3 series. In cross-examination PW 1 stated that the original khatian number of the suit land was 59 measuring an area of 55 acres. He also stated that Majam was the grandfather of plaintiff No. 1 Amiruddin. The RS record was prepared in the name of Nayan and. Baitullah father of the plaintiffs. At the time of settlement he was 17/18 years old. He was present at that time. He also stated the names of the persons who were present at the time of settlement. Alimuddin had written the amalnama except Yesmin Munshi other witnesses died. He denied that CS and RS records were correct. He denied that the notices in Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973 were served upon them. Yeasmin as PW 2 has corroborated the evidence of PW 1 in material particulars stating, inter alia, that Majam by an amalnama dated 12th Kartick 1344 BS granted settlement on 4.17 acres of land in favour of plaintiffs and he was present at the time of settlement. Amiruddin had written the amalnama. He also with Naimullah and Sabullah witnessed the amalnama. Majam put his thumb impression in the amalnama and on the same date issued a rent receipt which was written by Alimuddin. He proved the amalnama Exhibit 4 and rent receipts Exhibit 5 and other rent receipt marked Exhibit 5(Ka). The plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land. There are 5 homesteads in the suit land. In cross-examination he stated that he would be able to identify the hand writings of Alimuddin. He denied that amalnama was fraudulent and collusive document. He put his signature with a different pen in the Amalnama. In cross-examination he stated that he could not say exactly the plot numbers of the lands which were settled. He could not say the quantity of land on each of the plots possessed by the plaintiffs. Montaj Ali as PW 3 stated that he knew the suit land. The plaintiffs possessed the suit land by holding their homestead. In cross-examination he stated that the suit land was about 8/9 rashi apart from his house. The defendant Sonallah's house is situated on the suit land. The houses of Ashraf and Parullah are situated in the suit land. He could not say the exact number of the suit plots. Baderuddin as PW 4 in examination-in-chief stated that he knew the suit land. The plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land. The plaintiffs have been cultivating the suit land. In cross-examination he stated that his land is adjacent to the suit land. He could not say plot number, khatian number and area of the suit land. Sonaullah's house is situated on the suit land.

10. Abul Kashem as DW 1 stated that RS khatian was prepared in the name of Ebad and Ekram. He stated that RS record prepared without the names of Ebad and Ekram was wrong and that he filed Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973 which was decreed ex parte. The present plaintiffs were defendants in the Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973 and notices were duly served upon the defendants. He purchased the suit property with different sale deeds. He also deposed that RS record was correct. He denied that the plaintiffs are the owners of 4.17 acres of land. Amalnama and rent receipt filed by the plaintiffs were fraudulent and collusive documents. He proved the CS and RS khatian which were duly marked as Exhibits. In cross-examination he stated that the plaintiffs story of pattan is false. Out of the 6 plots Majam received his share measuring 1.14 acres. Remaining area of land are being possessed by the defendants. He denied that summons and notices of Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973 were suppressed and the ex parte decree was obtained collusively. In cross-examination he denied that the plaintiffs did not possess the suit land. He also denied that the plaintiffs have had their homestead in plot No. 955. In cross-examination, he stated that out of the suit land the plaintiffs possess plot No. 956 and remaining 5 plots were possessed by the defendants. He denied that he was deposing falsely. DW 2 in examination-in-chief stated that he knew the suit land. The plaintiffs possess the suit land in plot No. 956 and remaining land is being possessed by the other co-sharers. In cross-examination he denied that he had possessed illegally. DW 3 in cross-examination stated that he know the suit land which was comprising of 6 plots. The plaintiffs possess plot No. 956 and the remaining 5 plots were possessed by the other co-sharers. The defendants have their homestead in plot No. 955. In cross-examination DW 3 stated that he has no land adjacent to the suit land but his land is that suit land. He denied that he had not deposed falsely.

11. On consideration of the evidence of both sides and having pressed the judgments and decrees passed by the courts below it appears that the trial Court at the time of hearing of the case called for the records of Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973 and perused the same. On perusal of the same the learned Assistant Judge observed that “এ ব্যাপারে উক্ত মোকদ্দমার কাগজপত্র তলব করা হলে উহা রংপুর থেকে পাঠানো হয়। উক্ত মোকদ্দমার আরজি দৃষ্ট দেখা যায় অত্র মোকদ্দমার ১ ও ২ নং বাদী ১২৮৬/৭৩ ইং অন্য মোকদ্দমায় যথাক্রমে ১ও৭ নং বিবাদী ছিল। উক্ত মোকদ্দমার অর্ডার শীট দৃষ্টে দেখা যায় যে, তখন বাদী পক্ষের উপর বিবাদী হিসেবে সমন জারি হয়েছিল কিনা তার কোন উল্লেখ নেই। একটু বাদ ও দেখা যায যে সমস্ত সমন ১২৮৬/৭৩ ইং মোকদ্দমার ফেরত আসে ৩-১-৭৬ইং তারিখে অথচ মাত্র ১৬দিন পর অর্থাৎ ১৯-১-৭৬ ইং তারিখে বিবাদী পক্ষকে কোন সুযোগ না দিয়ে  একতরফা ডিক্রি হাসিল করা হয় । উপরের আলোচনা থেকে প্রতীয়মান হয় যে এক তরফা ডিক্রি হয় গত ১৯-১-৭৬  ইং তারিখে যা সঠিক ভাবে সম্পন্ন হয় নি । বাদী উক্ত একতরফা ডিক্রি রদ রহিত করে চাইয়া যে উপরের আলোচনা থেকে প্রতীয়মান হয় যে, পাইতে হক দার”

12. On careful perusal of the impugned judgment and decree it appears that the learned Additional District Judge as the appellate Court without reversing the aforesaid findings of the trial Court allowed the appeal and wrongly observed: “যেহেতু নালিশী জমিতে বাদী পক্ষ তাহাদির দাবীকৃত স্বত্ব ও একক দখল প্রমান করিতে সমর্থ হয় ন��ই। সেইহেতু উক্ত অন্য ১২৮৬/৭৩ ইং মোক্দ্দমার একতরফা ডিক্রি রহিত করিবার কোন সংগত কারণ দেখি না।

<u>13. Thus the Court of appeal below wrongly observed that there is no reason to set aside the ex parte decree since the plaintiffs failed to prove their title and possession in the suit land. Thereby the Court of appeal below committed an error of law in passing the impugned judgment and decree and in setting aside the judgment and decree by the learned Assistant Judge in Other Suit No. 56 of 1984 decreeing the suit and setting aside the ex parte decree passed in Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973. In the case reported in 5 MLR, 2 MLR and 50 DLR it has been consistently held that an ex parte decree may be set aside on the ground of non-service of summons upon the defendants and in the instant case the learned Assistant Judge having perused the case record of Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973 found that notices were not duly served upon the defendants. It is well established that an ex parte decree may be set aside on 2 grounds, namely, no service of summons upon the defendants or defendant was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing when the matter was called on and taken up for hearing. In the instant case the learned Assistant Judge found that service of summons were not duly served upon the defendants. There is no record of service of summons were duly served upon the defendants of Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973. In the case of Government of Bangladesh and another Vs Mashiur Rahman and others reported in 50 DLR (AD) 205 it has been observed that when an ex parte decree is challenged on ground of being obtained by fraud, and some elements of fraud and collusion are found on the record, the court is not to sustain such fraudulent decree even if an application seeking the setting aside of the ex parte decree is barred by limitation. In the decision of the case of Alauddin Khan vs Mohammad Sheikh & others reported in 2 MLR 383 wherein it has been held that in order to sustain an ex parte decree the decree holder must prove that the summons upon the defendants were duly served. It is found that the ex parte decree is liable to be set aside even if the defendants had knowledge about the institution of the suit. In the instant case it appears that the plaintiffs-petitioners who were the defendants in Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973 denied the service of summons. In the circumstances of onus lies upon the plaintiffs of Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973 (i.e the present opposite parties) to prove that the summons were duly served upon the defendants (i.e. the present petitioner). But in instant case the present opposite parties failed to prove that summons were duly served upon the present petitioners in Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973. Other defendants also failed to prove other aspect of the matter and failed to prove that there is no reason to set aside the ex parte decree and, as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged.</u>

<u>14. As regards title and possession of the plaintiff-petitioners it appears that plaintiff No. 2 as PW 1 adduced evidence in support of their contention. It is also admitted by the defendants that the plaintiffs are in possession of some portion of the suit land and PW 2 also admitted that one of the defendant's house is adjacent to the suit land. On careful perusal of the evidence of the witnesses of both sides it appears that both the plaintiffs and the defendants are in possession of different portion of the suit land. As regards document of title the plaintiffs proved their title by unregistered amalnama dated 12th Kartick, 1344 BS and some rent receipts. The defendants-opposite-parties deposed that these were antedated, fraudulent and collusive documents. PW 2 in cross examination stated that the plaintiffs paid education tax, irrigation tax in 1344 BS. The learned Court of appeal below held that no such taxes were available in 1344 BS. The Court of appeal below could not believe the authenticity of the 1346 BS rent receipts and the amalnama and the Court of appeal found that the amalnama said to have been written by fountain pen in 1344 was not genuine and that it was not prevalent to write with fountain pen at that time. But in this case it appears that the witnesses of the plaintiffs like PWs 1 and 2 were attesting witnesses of the amalnama in whose presence the settlement was taken. By cross-examining these PWs the defendants could not find out any departure in the evidence of both witnesses. Though it was the case of the defendants-opposite-parties that the amalnama and rent receipt were fraudulent and collusive documents yet with the evidence of the DWs they could not prove any fraudulent and forged documents. But in cross-examination PW 2 stated that while paying land revenue for 1344 BS they paid different taxes including education tax and cess tax. It also appears from the evidence of witnesses that Majam was the grandfather of plaintiff No. 1 and they claimed suit property through the amalnama and rent receipts. None of the members of his family and other heirs of Majam raised any dispute regarding the authenticity of the amalnama and rent receipts. Though the defendants challenged the authenticity of the amalnama and rent receipts yet they failed to discharge the burden on them to prove that these documents were fraudulent and collusive documents but the Court of appeal below made out a 3rd case that the education tax and case tax were not levied in the year 1344 BS. So the Court of appeal below disbelieved the rent receipts. It is difficult to understand what prompted the Court of appeal below to say that no amalnama was written by fountain pen in this part of the world in 1344 BS. The defendants-petitioners could have adduced evidence to that effect in proving that fountain pen was not available on or before 1344 BS or the amalnama in question was not written by fountain pen in 1344 BS and in that case the Court of appeal below could have made such remark. But on mere surmises and conjectures the Court of appeal below on misconceived view held that fountain pen was not used in 1344 BS and the amalnama and the tent receipts were not written with fountain pen. It appears that the Court of appeal below committed an error of law in making such observation without any basis which has resulted in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. But on careful perusal of the evidence of witnesses of both the parties it appears that the Court of appeal below rightly found that the plaintiffs are not in exclusive possession of 4.17 acres of land and both the parties are in ejmali possession of the suit land. In that view of the matter the title of the co-sharers in the joint property cannot be declared without making partition of the joint property. For the aforesaid reasons, I am of the opinion that the Court of appeal below rightly dismissed the prayer of the plaintiff-petitioners for declaration of title in the suit land. The plaintiffs-petitioners are at liberty to seek appropriate relief in a property suit. We have already noticed that the plaintiffs-petitioners proved that summons and notices of Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973 were not duly served upon them (ie defendants of that suit). In that view of the matter I am of the opinion that the Court of appeal below committed an error of law in not finding that summons and notices of Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973 were not duly served upon the present petitioners (i.e. the defendants of that suit) which has resulted in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice and that the Court of appeal below should have affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court so far as it relates to the setting aside the judgment and decree dated 19-1-1976 passed in Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973. So, I am of the view that the plaintiffs petitioners partly succeed.</u>

15. In the result, the Rule is made absolute in part without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge in Other Appeal No. 94 of 1999, so far as it relates to the setting aside the judgment and decree dated 5-8-1999 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Rawmari in other suit No. 56 of 1984 in setting aside the ex parte judgment and decree dated 19-1-1976 passed by the learned Munsif Kurigram. The Other Suit No. 1286 of 1973 is hereby set aside and the impugned judgment and decree so far as it relates to the setting aside the judgment and decree dated 5-8-1999 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Rawmari, Kurigram. In other suit No. 56 of 1984 decreeing the suit for declaration of title of the plaintiffs is hereby affirmed.

Communicate the order at once to the learned Courts below with the copy of this judgment.

End.

full_judgment:
AHM Shamsuddin Chowdhury J : This appeal from original order is directed against the judgment and the order dated 13-4-1998 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Commercial Court, Chittagong in Other Suit No. 3 of 1998 refusing to grant temporary injunction.

2. Other Suit No. 3 of 1998 came into being following the filing of a plaint whereby the plaintiff prayed for (1) a decree of declaration to the effect that the plaintiff is not liable to pay technical fee to defendant No. 1, (2) a decree for Taka 4240165.46 in favour of the plaintiff and against the defendant No. 1. One Salauddin Ahmed, proprietor of M/s Green Aro, was impleaded as defendant No. 1, while Janata Bank, Foreign Exchange Corporate Branch, CDA Annex Building, Chittagong, was made defendant No. 2.

3. The filing of the suit was followed by an application for temporary injunction under Order XXXIX rules 1 and 2 and section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The temporary injunction prayer was aimed to prevent the defendant No.1 from receiving and defendant No. 2 from paying what is called technical fee, payable to the defendant’s No. 1.

4. The gist of the relevant averments as made in the temporary injunction petition are narrated hereinafter. The defendant No. 1 carries on the business as local representative and agent of foreign purchaser as well as of suppliers of fabrics and accessories. This business is popularly known as the business of Buying House. Such a house generally obtains order for exporting abroad garments through letters of credit (LC) which are established in its name by foreign buyers. The business includes establishing contacts with supplier's fabrics and accessories, negotiation with the garments manufacturer, fixation of the sale and purchase of fabrics and garments. In consideration of these services it is paid, what is called, technical fees, the amount of which fees are mentioned in the Master Export LC.

5. In this particular case defendant No. obtained a Master Export LC dated 11-12-1995 opened by Ely and Sidney Limited of the United Kingdom, through FIBI Bank (UK) PLC for an amount of US Dollars 1,139,750 for exporting 50,000 (this figure is obviously wrong because the LC says US$ 1,139,750.00 for 8000 dozens) dozens of cotton knitted Basic T .Shirts. The defendant No.1, after fruitful negotiation with the plaintiff transferred part value of the said Master LC to the tune of US Dollars 745,000 to the plaintiff for cutting and manufacturing 50,000, dozens of cotton knitted Basic T shirts by the plaintiff @ US$ 1.40 per dozen. At the instruction of the defendant No. 1 the plaintiff then opened one Import LC in favour of Orient Fabrics and Garments Ltd for an amount of US Dollars 546178.02 for the importation of fabric from the said company and another Import LC for US Dollars 12,500 for importing accessories from Royal Thread Industries. Prices for the said fabrics and accessories were fixed through negotiation between the defendant No.1 and the said suppliers. The plaintiff states that the defendant No.1 being the local representative of the buyer as well as of the suppliers and being the transferor of the Master Export LC is to take all necessary steps to ensure supply of proper quality fabrics within stipulated time for which he is paid fees known as technical fees. This technical service of the defendant No. 1 include importation of proper quantity of fabrics in time, supervision of manufacturing, packing, exporting, shipping of the garments in time, realisation of export bills as well as payment of import bills.

6. Although the accessories were received by the plaintiff within the LC validity period the fabrics were not so received. After repeated extension of time, the supplier of fabrics eventually delivered only 37,000 kgs of fabrics out of stipulated quantity of 1, 10, 183 kgs and then again, they were very defective in various ways. The defendant No.1 and the garments (should be fabrics) supplier assured of compensation and advised the plaintiff to open another LC in favour of another company for importing the unsupplied quantity of fabrics, which the plaintiff had to do with a huge loss. Due to belated delivery of the fabrics, due to inadequacy of supply and also due to defective qualities of the same and due to other incidental consequences arising from the said maladies, the plaintiff suffered substantial economic loss and damage of various descriptions. The plaintiff further stated that because of the said breaches he could manufacture only 25730 dozens out of 50000 dozens and could ship only 10800 dozens within the LC validity period, and the export bill of the fabrics was also not paid in time and for the balance of unexpected quantity of garments the defendant No. 1 could not get the LC validity extended and consequently, the plaintiff had to export the same at his own risk on collection basis sustaining a loss of US$ 14930.00 because of his UK visit. The plaintiff claimed that the loss that he had to suffer was due to the defendant No. 1's inability to complete the transaction as per the terms of the Master LC and, as such, the plaintiff incurred loss of Taka 42,40,165.46 and, as such, the defendant No.1 is not entitled to get technical fee. At another place of the injunction petition it has been stated that the defendant No. 1 cannot get technical fees and is liable to compensate the plaintiff as he failed to perform technical services. The plaintiff further stated that taking advantage of the imprintment of technical fees in the LC the defendant No. 1 instead of settling the dispute through arbitration to which he previously agreed started creating pressure on defendant No. 2 bank for the payment of technical fees. In view of the defendant No. 1’s persistent: pressure and in the face of defendant No. 2's threat that it would pay to the defendant No. 1 the fees as per the terms of the export LC, the plaintiff has been compelled to file the suit.

7. The learned Judge below summarily rejected the temporary injunction petitions stating that such an injunction would be contrary to the principles narrated in the case of Sarhind Garments Ltd vs Glory Truth Industries Ltd and others 49 DLR 260.

8. Mr Musta Niaz Muhammad, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff/appellant, admitting that the payment of technical fee is the responsibility of the overseas principal of the defendant No. 1 namely Elly & Sidney Limited, i.e. the buyers of the garments and not that of the plaintiff, submitted that as the defendant No. 1 has no other property, asset or liquid cash to satisfy any possible decree, it has become absolutely essential to prevent the payment of the technical fees. He submitted that once the payment is made the decree or declaration to the effect that the defendant No. 1 is not entitled to pay any technical fee, shall become meaningless. He further submitted that the plaintiff has an interest in the disputed money which is designated as technical fee in that if the plaintiff succeeds in obtaining a decree in the suit, the said technical fee amount will remain intact for the defendant No. 1 to be able to honour such a decree. He further submitted that inasmuch as the defendant No. 1 has nothing else, the plaintiff shall suffer irreparable loss if the defendant No. 1 is allowed to receive the amount designated as technical fees in the letter of credit. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff/appellant submitted that the money is, nevertheless, earmarked for defendant No. 1 and, as such, the payment and receipt of the same could be restrained by an order of injunction.

9. Mr Khandaker Mahbubuddin, the Senior Counsel for the plaintiff/appellant, who commenced his submission at a later stage, contended the decisions in the case of Sarhind Garments vs Glory Truth Industries Ltd reported in 49 DLR 260 and in the case of Uttara Bank vs Macneill and Kilburn Ltd and others reported in 33 DLR (AD) 298, were only relevant to cases where the letters of credit were in respect to international transaction, whereas in the present case, the transaction is very much a domestic one and the parties to the dispute are also based in this country. He also submitted that what was sought to be injuncted was not the LC itself but the payment of a quoted amount of money therefrom to the defendant No. 1 and hence the letter of credit itself was not sought to be the subject matter of the injunction and, as such, these decisions were not applicable at all. He contended that hence there was nothing to impede the issuance of an order of injunction. He submitted that the plaintiff sought to ensure the effectiveness of a possible decree for which the plaintiff has filed the suit. He further submitted that inasmuch as the defendant No. 1 has no other money or property to honour any possible decree that may be passed in favour of the plaintiff, the question of adequacy of pecuniary compensation is but a utopia.

10. In reply, Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud for the defendant respondent emphatically argued that the plaintiff appellant has no personal right or interest in the money in dispute in that it is not him who is responsible for the payment of the technical fees. Citing section 56(k) of the Specific Relief Act he contended that the plaintiffs’ lack of right and interest in the money is in itself enough for the appeal to end up in dismissal. He further argued that no injunction can lie without making Ely & Sidney Ltd a party in the suit inasmuch as the payment of technical fees is the exclusive responsibility of that company. He submitted that as the money in the letter of credit is designated as technical fee payable to the defendant No. 1, the same shall revert back to the person whom it emanated from, in the event the money does not for any reason, reach the said defendant. Mr Mahmud argued that the plaintiff/appellant has failed to make out a prima facie case, submitting further that as per the decision reported in 33 DLR (AD) 298, to make a letter of credit immune from injunctive order, it is not necessary to show that parties to the suit are based in different countries. He went on submitting that in any event the LC in dispute falls within the category of international transaction because it arose out of a business dealing between parties based in two different countries, it was issued by a bank in London while the Negotiating Bank was a Bangladeshi one, the person at whose instance the LC was issued is based in the UK while the recipients are in Bangladesh. Mr Mahmud concludes by submitting that what will be the outcome of the suit remains a hypothetical question at this stage, but if the plaintiff appellant does succeed to get the decrees prayed for he will have a better chance of realising the decretal amount if the defendant No. 1's technical fees are released, because in that event the said defendant would be financially better off to pay such a decretal amount. He however, submitted that no such chance of success is apparent from prima facie evidence.

11. The plaintiff/appellant's case, in short, is that insofar as the defendant No. 1 failed to perform his part of the obligation diligently causing loss to the plaintiff and as he did not render technical services he is not entitled to get the technical fees, and that as one of the two prayers in the plaint, i.e. prayer (a) is for a declaration to the effect that the defendant No. 1 is not entitled to the technical fee, any relief granted on the said prayer shall be rendered infructuous if the technical fee is paid to the said defendant before the disposal of the suit, and hence an interlocutory measure to stop such payment is indispensable. The appellant's learned Senior Advocate put all the more emphasis on the contention that since the plaintiff appellant has no other asset a possible decree in favour of the plaintiff appellant shall become brutum fulmen.

<u>12. In addition to the question of applicability of the principles reiterated in the case of Uttara Bank vs Macneill and Kilburn Ltd 33 DLR (AD) 289 and in the case of Sarhind Garments vs Glory Truth Industries Ltd and others 49 DLR 260, two other pertinent questions that attract our attention are (I) as to whether the plaintiff has any interest in the money he aspires to injunct and (2) what is the legal nature of the relationship between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 inter se? The question No.(1) above invariably raises the question as to whose responsibility is it to pay technical fee. Through prayer (a) in the plaint the plaintiff has prayed for a declaration to the effect that he is not liable to pay technical fee to the defendant No. 1 because of the breaches committed by the latter. This prayer denotes that it is the plaintiff who is responsible for the payment of technical fee. But the said claim seems to be paradoxical in view of the consistent assertion by the plaintiff that the defendant No. 1 acted as the agent of the overseas buyer of garments as well as of the overseas supplier of fabrics and accessories. Under the law of agency the agent is paid by his principal only. He cannot be paid any commission by the opposite party, because an agent owes his contractual duty to his principal only, and indeed, the agent will be in a situation of conflict of interest and dishonesty if he receives any remuneration from the third party (Anglo African Merchants Ltd vs Sayley 1970 1 QB-311; Cook vs Deeks 1916 1 AC 554). Such receipt may be tantamount to underhand dealing, unless of course, it is stipulated between the principal and the other party that the responsibility of making payment of commission to the agent shall lie, not on the principal but on the other party. Nothing like that could be found in this case. Paragraph 15 of the plaint as well as the document produced as Annexure-A(3) also suggest that in the present case the responsibility of paying the agent's commission rested on his principal. Paragraph 15 (bottom) of the plaint reads, "In the nature of the said trade, the entire profit from the supply of the fabrics and export of garments is enjoyed by the supplier of the fabrics, purchaser of the garments and their local representative known as Buying House, the defendant No. 1. The manufacturer of the garments i.e., plaintiff, receive only fixed cutting and manufacturing (CM) charge." It is too difficult, in view of the said statement of fact, to accept that commission to the agent of the other side should be payable by the manufacturer who, according to his own statement, receives only fixed cutting and manufacturing charges. The document marked as Annexure A(3) by which the defendant No. 1. intimated the plaintiff about the transfer of the part LC value, which document contains a breakdown of different amounts of money payable to different business concerns from the total transferred amount of US$ 745,000.00. The breakdown shows that out of the total amount of US$ 745,000.00 transferred to the plaintiff CM (Cutting and manufacturing) charge of US$ 70000.00 only was to go to the plaintiff, while US$ 546178.02, US$ 12500.00 and. US$ 116321.98 were payable respectively, to the suppliers of fabrics, supplier of accessories and to the defendant No. 1. It is therefore, clear that all the money payable to different concerns inclusive of the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 as his technical fees actually came from defendant No. 1's principal in the UK through a documentary credit. From the above stated scenario it is impossible to reconcile with the claim that the technical fee emanated from the plaintiff. It also suggest that even the plaintiffs own CM charges were handed over to him by the defendant No.1 because it is the defendant No. 1 who was the original beneficiary of the LC and who actually transferred a part of his interest in the LC to the plaintiff with specific data of each person's rights in the money. Indeed, it was open to the said defendant to create four instruments of transferred credits for four different beneficiaries, including himself, although possibly for the sake of convenience, and to enable the plaintiff of open back to back LC in favour of the fabrics and accessories suppliers with the backing of the Master Export LC he created only one instrument of Transferred LC. It can also be said that the , defendant No. 1 at the time of the said transfer, effectively retained to himself his technical fee by specifically stating so not only in the said exhibit A(3) but also the very endorsement, which was the basis of the transfer. Accordingly, the plaintiffs’ right is restricted to US$ 70000 only. It does then follow as a natural corollary that if, other people mentioned in Annexure A (3) for any reason render themselves unfit to receive- the stipulated amount, even then the money earmarked for them cannot legally go to the plaintiffs pocket, but should revert back to whence it came i.e. to Elly and Sideney Ltd. Mr Mustafa Niaz Muhammad, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff, also very candidly, accepted that in the event of the defendant No. 1's disqualification, for any reason to receive the said money, the same should go back to the overseas buyer at whose behest the Master Export LC was opened, through the issuing bank. We believe that it will not be wrong to say that if the plaintiff takes any amount beyond US$ 70000 such an action will be tantamount to misappropriation for the reason that the defendant No.1, who originally owned the entire amount of credit, transferred US$ 70000 only to the plaintiff by specifying that only US$ 70000 was for the plaintiff. As far as the defendant No.1’s US$ 1 I 6321.98 is concerned, the same was meant to be handed over to the said defendant by the negotiating bank (defendant No.2) itself, before the said bank parted with the remainder of the money. If the money in dispute had not fountained from the plaintiff and if the same cannot lawfully be redirected to him, in the event other beneficiaries fail to receive it, we are afraid, we remain unconvinced that the plaintiff does have a legal right or interest over the money.</u>

13. The indispensability of the presence of plaintiffs right in the subject matter of injunction prayer have been demonstrated in a number of English decisions of universal significance. In the widely acclaimed case of Gouriet vs Attorney General (1978 AC 435) the House of Lords stated that a plaintiff with no right on the subject matter, cannot obtain an injunction, however, just and convenient it may be. In Paton vs British Pregnancy Advisory Services Trustees (1979 QB 276) Sir George Baker, the President of the Family Division, insisted that to qualify for an injunctory relief, the plaintiff must show that he holds a legal right, enforceable in law or in equity. Curiously, in the latter case a husband's prayer for an injunction to prevent his wife and the medical practitioners from legally aborting the foetus in the wife's womb, was turned down on the ground that the husband lacked such a legal right. So, this appeal is liable to be dismissed as Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud argued for plaintiff’s lack of legal right or interest alone.

<u>14. The nature of legal relationship between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1, if any, is yet another crucial question. The plaintiff consistently and persistently asserted that the defendant No. 1 is a representative and agent of overseas buyers of garments and suppliers of fabrics. If that be correct then the plaintiffs claim that the defendant No. 1 is not entitled to any technical fee because he failed to render technical services, loses all its legal significance for the reason that if he acted for his principal, then the question as to the said party's entitlement to the technical fee is definitely a matter between him and his principal. In his petition, the plaintiff claimed that he suffered loss because of defendant No.1’s breaches and that is why he said defendant cannot get any technical fee. In. this respect one has to keep in mind, as has been stated by Cheshire and Fiffot in their- book "Law of Contract", 13th edition, page 483, "the general rule is not only that the principal acquires rights and liabilities, but also that the agent drops out and ceases to be a party to the contract," if he acts qua agent. The principal is bound, as regards third parties, by all the acts of the agent under the maxim "Qui facit per alium, facit per se. " Anson's Law of Contract, Twenty-fifth edition, page 626, states, "since an agent is employed to establish privity of contract between his principal and a third party, it is the general rule that he acquires no rights and incurs no liability." He can of course be used by his principal under "agent-principal" contractual relationship (White vs Lincoln 1803, 8 Yes. Jun 363). But he is not himself a party to any contract entered into by his principal through him with a third party if he posed as a disclosed agent of his principal and, as such, no question of his liability to such a third party for any breach can arise. There are, however a few circumstances of exception where an agent can be liable. These exceptions include a situation (1) when an agent is a party to a deed, not as a constituted attorney, but as a party, (2) if he signs negotiable instrument without authority, (3) if principal is non-existent, (4) if the agent is guilty of misrepresentation, (5) if he does not disclose existence of any principal and projects himself as the principal, (6) if he acts without authority, (7) if he expressly or impliedly assumes personal liability, (8) if trade usage or customs make him liable, (9) if he actually contracts on his own behalf,(10) if he refuses to identify the principal. It is always a question of construction by which the presumed intention of the parties is to be assessed, as far as available from the circumstances. Such an intention, if clearly evident, is decisive, but if not, the general principle shall apply which dictates that the contract is the contract of the principal, not that of the agent, and prima facie in law the only person who can be sued is the principal (Montgomerie vs United Kingdom Mutual SS Association 1891, I QB 370). In Pacquin vs Beanclerk (1906 AC 148) also it was observed that an agent possesses neither rights nor liabilities. This is more so if the agency is a disclosed one. A disclosed agency therefore, creates a refutable presumption that it is the principal, and not the agent, who is the contracting party. The prima facie rule that if the contract is made for a named principal then the principal alone can sue or be sued, is however a refutable presumption of purely general character. At one time, it used to be perceived that a person who contracted for a foreign principal should be regarded as having contracted as a principal to the exclusion of foreign principal (Elbinger AG Fur Fabrication Von Fisonbahn Material vs Clay-1873 LR, 8 QB 313). But with the vast increase in international trade, this particular usage has steadily waned and has now disappeared (Teheran-Euro Ltd vs ST Belton (Tractor) Ltd 1986, 2 All ER 886). No doubt the plaintiff will have ample opportunity to try to resolve the dichotomy arising from terming the defendant No.1 as an agent on the one hand and trying to impose contractual. liability on him on the other hand, at the time of the trial by adducing evidence and advancing intrinsic legal submission and, perhaps by showing that the defendant No. 1 falls within one of the exceptions, but as far as we are concerned, and insofar as it is an appeal against the rejection of temporary injunction application, only with limited affidavit evidence before us, we found nothing to enable us to deviate from the general principle and we take such a state of affairs as the plaintiffs failure to make out a prime facie case.</u>

15. Our above described conclusions are enough to dismiss this appeal. However, in view of the finding of the learned Judge below that granting of an injunction would be contrary to the principles elucidated in the case of Sarhind Garments Ltd vs Glory Truth Industries Ltd and another; (49 DLR 260), we feel constrained to analyse the principles enunciated in that case, to see if they are applicable in the present case. In Sarhind Garments this Division followed the principles reiterated by the Indian Supreme Court in Tarapore and Co vs Tractorexport, Moscow (AIR 1970 (SC) 891), which principles were also cited with approval in Uttara Bank vs Macneil and Kilburn Ltd and others (33 DLR (AD) 298. At the very inception, we should clarify that, as Mr Khandaker rightly pointed out, the factual characteristic of the present case is quite different from the factual characteristic in the cases of Sarhind Garments, Uttara Bank and those other cases which have been referred to in these two cases. Facts in Sarhind Garments and Tarapore cases were straight forward. The buyers sought temporary injunction to prevent the Issuing Banks from paying, and the sellers from receiving money as per the terms of the LCs opened at buyers instruction, on the plea that the sellers could not receive the said money because they have been in breach of those underlying contracts which culminated in the issuance of the LCs. Factual nature of the present case is by no means, similar and simple. Here the plaintiff is neither the buyer nor the promoter of the LC but a seller who seeks to prevent payment of money, not representing price of supplied goods, but agent's commission, which the negotiating bank is proposing to pay, to a person, who is neither the seller nor the buyer, but, according to the plaintiffs pleadings, is an agent of an overseas buyer, who was instrumental to bring about a contractual relationship between the said overseas buyer on the one side and the plaintiff/seller on the other side, the said foreign buyer, not being a party to the suit. Moreover, in this case, the bank against which injunction is being sought is the Negotiating Bank, not the Issuing Bank. Furthermore, the disputed amount of defendant No. 1's technical fee was not specified by the Issuing Bank, which made the said defendant beneficiary of the entire LC amount, but was specified by the said defendant himself by an endorsement to that effect at the time he transferred part value of the LC to the plaintiff.

<u>16. In view of the said divergence of factual circumstances, we had to examine the ratio of the decisions in Sarhind Garments Case, as well as in the case of Tarapore and Co vs Tractorexport, Moscow (AIR 1970 SC 891). In Uttara Bank vs MacneiL and Kilburn Ltd, where the facts are somewhat different in that, a letter of guarantee, issued by a local bank at the instruction of a local seller in favour of a local bank of a local buyer, was sought to be injuncted by the seller, the Appellate Division cited with approval the principles elaborated in Tarapore Case. What emerged from Sarhind Garments and Tarapore Cases, cited above, in a nutshell, are (1) that in the field of international trade, a buyer, pursuant to his agreement with the seller, instructs a bank, known as Issuing Bank, to open a letter of credit designating the seller as the beneficiary, and making the credit available to the seller abroad, so that the seller feels sure and confident that he will get his money, (2) that when the issuing bank opens such a letter of credit and informs the seller/beneficiary of the said issuance, a contractual nexus comes into being between the Issuing Bank and the seller/beneficiary, whereby the Issuing Bank undertakes an absolute liability to pay the credit amount on production of such documents which are stated in the credit creating instrument, (3) that the said contractual nexus between the Issuing bank and the beneficiary of the credit, is, though ancillary to the underlying or the principal contract, between the seller and the buyer, a separate, distinct and independent contractual nexus, in that the right and the duty to pay the beneficiary as per the terms of the letter of credit has nothing to do with the performance, non-performance, negligent performance, omission to perform, any duty which the beneficiary is obligated to perform under the terms of the underlying contract, he may have entered into with the person at whose instance the letter of credit was issued, (4) that, unless there is compelling evidence of fraud the Courts will not grant an injunction. It was also emphasised that the assurance of payment given through banker’s documentary credit is a mechanism of international trade which will have adverse effect on such trade if interfered with. So, the essence, of the above discussed decisions are, that the Courts, except on compelling evidence of fraud, will not grant an injunction to prevent the bank from paying the beneficiary such amount of money which the issuing bank is absolutely promise bound to pay by having issued a letter of credit or a guarantee, even if the beneficiary has not done, or has done imperfectly, what he is contract bound to do for the person at whose instruction the credit was created and, that is essentially because the contract by which the bank is so obligated, is quite independent of any underlying or principal contract, and also because the Court's interference with a recognised mechanism of international trade would have repercussion on such trade. In the language of their Lordships in Sarhind Garments Case "A letter of credit has an autonomy of its own and it needed to be negotiated without reference to the very contract out of which the credit arises." Albeit factual difference, the Appellate Division in Uttara Bank case approved the above principle.</u>

17. It is, in this context, worth mentioning that irrevocable letters of credit have received exceptional status, possibly because of the unique role it plays in international trade, from the Courts all over the world, in that, by way of an exception to a cardinal principle of the law of contract, the issuance of irrevocable letters of credit generate contractual obligation on the promisor despite total lack of consideration from the promisee, which exceptional treatment provoked Prof MR Goode to say, "The problem is to reconcile the binding nature of the bank's undertaking with traditional concept of general law, which deny legal effect to a simple promise unless consideration is furnished by the promisee, producing a contract. The difficulty created by the undertaking embodied in an irrevocable letter of credit is, that it appears to be binding on the issuing bank and enforceable by seller despite the fact that S has furnished no consideration for issuing bank's promise and, indeed, may not have taken steps to act upon it, nor even have signified his assent to its terms." (Prof MR Goode's Commercial Law, page 658). Prof Ellinger has however, suggested a compromise by arguing that the letter of credit should be treated as a "sui generis instrument, "embodying a promise which, by mercantile usage, is enforceable without consideration. Be it as it may, the stark reality is that despite the conspicuous absence of an indispensable requirement, namely, consideration, it is now beyond qualm that the theory that the Issuing Bank is contract bound to honour its promise, despite absence of consideration from the promisee, has received judicial recognition universally.

18. Autonomy of the "paying bank-beneficiary" contract from the underlying or the principal contract is then the crux of the matter. So, in spite of significant dissimilarity in factual nature, the principles in Uttara Bank case, Sarhind Garments case would apply, in the present case, only if it is obvious, that an independent contractual nexus was established between the negotiating bank (defendant No. 2) and the defendant No. 1. This requires us to look at the transaction at some length.

19. In the instant case a UK-based bank called FIBI Bank Ltd issued an irrevocable and transferable letter of credit which was also a "sight" credit, at the instruction of a UK-based buyer named Elly & Sidney Ltd. According to the plaintiffs pleadings, the latter company is defendant No. 1's principal. The defendant No. 1 was the sole beneficiary in the pre-transfer letter of credit. On receipt of the credit, the said defendant transferred an amount of US$ 745,000 to the plaintiff, which was only a part value of the entire credit amount of US$ 1139750 granted by the said instrument for 80000 dozens of garments. The transfer was authenticated by the United Commercial Bank in accordance with Article 48 of the Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credit (UCP) complied by International Chamber of Commerce (lCC). Although the widely used UCP provisions in themselves do not have any force of law under the general principles of the law of contract, they become part of a contract if the parties agree to incorporate those provisions in their contract. As the UCP 500 provisions were incorporated in the contracts generating from the letter of credit, the UPC 500 provisions are part of the concerned contracts. Article 48(a) of the UCP-500, reads "A transferable credit is a credit under which the beneficiary (First Beneficiary) may request the bank authorised to pay, incur a deferred payment undertaking, accept or negotiate (the Transferring Bank), or in the case of a freely negotiable credit, the bank specifically authorised in the credit as a Transferring Bank, to make the credit available in whole or in part to one or more other Beneficiary(ies) (Second Beneficiary (ies)".

20. In the present case United Commercial Bank Ltd, by authenticating the transfer at defendant No. 1's request became the Transferring Bank as per Article 48 UCP 500. The Transferring Bank however caused the transfer on the basis of the terms embodied in the endorsement made by defendant No.1, because the said endorsement constituted the very foundation of the transfer. The endorsement runs as follows: "Without any risk and responsibility on our part, we do hereby transfer the UC No.LC 22800 Dt ll-12-95 for part value of USD 745000 'only to Mission Appeal Industries, FIDC ROAD BSCIC IIE. Kalurghat, Chittagong. Covering shipment of style # ES-140 white 30000 Doz; ES-140 MEL 20000 Doz of 100% Cotton knitted basic T-Shirts.

The Negotiating Bank will pay credit USD 2.018 Doz on style No.ES-140 white and USD 2. 789099/Doz on style No.ES 140 MEL. IE Total USD 116321.98 on Total above quantity as technical fee to Green ARO, CD A/C No. 33034573, United Commercial Bank, Jubilee Road branch, Chittagong. Pre-Shipment Inspection Certificate will be issued and signed by Salahuddin Ahmed of Green Aro and it must be verified by the Transferring Bank Commercial invoice must show local buying agent Green Aro, 5, Zakir, Hossain Road, Khulsi, Chittagong."

21. The said endorsement, by which the defendant No. I became the donor and the plaintiff became he recipient of some money under the credit, established no less than four separate, distinct, independent and autonomous contractual relationships. Meticulous dissection of two of such contractual nexus is of utmost importance for the disposal of the present appeal. They are the contracts, (1) between the defendant No.1 on the one side and the Negotiating Bank (defendant No. 2) on the other side and (II) the Transferring Bank on the one side and Negotiating Bank (defendant No.2) on the other. It goes without saying that the second paragraph of the endorsement, which reads, "The Negotiating Bank will pay/credit Green Aro ...........was obviously addressed to the Negotiating Bank and was indeed a "Proposal" within the scope of section 2(a) of the Contract Act. The defendant No.2 (Janata Bank) having agreed to negotiate the transferred letter of credit and by actually acting on the said letter of credit, accepted the said proposal whereby a contractual nexus was established between the defendant No.1 and the defendant No.2 bank, by reason of the fact that all the three essential elements of a contract namely, (a) proposal (b) acceptance and (c) consideration (banks commission) were present. In this context we wish to reiterate that the immortal decision in the nineteenth century case of Carlill vs Carbolic Smoke Ball C (1893.1 QB 256), despite passage of time, still stand, unimpeached, as an authority for the proposition that an offer need not be made to a named person, but can be addressed to the whole world and that though, as a general rule, acceptance must be communicated, no. communication is necessary if the offer expressly or impliedly dispenses with the requirement to communicate or if the terms of the offer are such that acceptance is caused by acting upon the offer, as was done by the defendant No. 2 in this case by acting on the transferred LC. By considering the principles, as narrated in Sarhind Garments, and Tarapore cases, and, as cited with approval in Uttara Bank Case, it can be said that the contract as established between the defendant No. 1 and the defendant No. 2, in the present case, is also separate and autonomous from any underlying contract and, as such, despite wide differences in factual character, the said principles should apply to the present case. Accordingly, no injunctory order should be granted, either to prevent the payment, or to prevent the receipt, of the said amount of US$ 113261.98. As was emphasised in Contax (India) vs Vinmar Impex Inc (AIR 1986 (SC) 1924), the commitment of the bank must be allowed to be honoured free of interference by the courts as otherwise trust in international commerce would be irreparably tarnished. The Court below did not, therefore, commit any error in rejecting the Quia Timet temporary injunction application on LC contract ground, though the Order of the learned court below should have been a speaking Order.

22. The same principle would also apply as far as the Transferring Bank-Negotiating Bank (defendant No. 2) contract is concerned, inasmuch as that contract is also totally separate, independent, distinct and autonomous from any underlying contract, wherefore the defendant No. 2 is contractually obligated to the Transferring Bank to pay the money in dispute to the defendant No. 1, notwithstanding the defendant No.1's inability to enforce this particular contract by himself because of the doctrine of "Privity of Contract" (Beswick vs. Beswick (1968 AC 58). So, no injunction can be granted, following the above discussed principles, to prevent the defendant No.2 from paying the defendant No. 1 US$ 116321.98 even under the "Transferring Bank-Defendant No.2" contract as well.

23. Albeit the parties to the present litigation are in Bangladesh and the money in dispute is also here, the other principle, as illuminated in Tarapore and Sarhind Garments cases i.e. the principle of non-interference with a fundamental mechanism of international trade, is, in our view, applicable in the present case as equal by reason of the fact that the system of transferring letters of credit has, by now, gained sufficient ground to be reckoned as an important mechanism in the international trade of ready-made garments, interference with which mechanism is bound to have adverse repercussions on our country's international trade involving garments export. It must also be kept in mind that no distinction between international trade and internal trade was drawn in the Uttara Bank Case in highlighting Court's reluctance to interfere with commercial transactions through performance of guarantee.

24. So far as the question of irreparability of loss is concerned, Mr Khandaker Mahbubuddin, in his characteristic ingenious style of advocation, submitted that if the defendant No. 1 possessess no money, the question of adequacy of financial compensation would be a sham one. Traditionally "inadequacy of financial compensation" or "irreparable loss" is meant to indicate a kind of a loss which cannot be measured in terms of money, in other words, a loss that cannot be repaired by money. Although, Mr Khandaker Mahbubuddin's submission, visibly, resulted from his own idea par excellence, without reliance on any authority, there is no paucity of authorities to support his view and the view that the phrase "irreparability of loss" is not necessarily confined to a situation where monetary compensation is deemed insufficient. The phrase goes beyond that limit and also embraces a situation where remedy available from the Common Law is nominal, or cumbersome to obtain or where monetary award will be faced with insurmountable problem or impossibility, so far as the realisation of the same will be concerned. The case of Morning Star Co-operative Society Ltd vs Express Newspapers Ltd (The Times October 18. 1978) is a direct authority to lend support to Mr Khandaker's contention. It was observed in the quoted case that pecuniary compensation will be deemed to be inadequate if an individual defendant does not have the means to pay any appreciable damages. In Evans Marshall & Co Ltd vs Bertola SA (1973 1 WLR 349), it was stated that pecuniary damages would be inadequate if the defendant is a foreign company whose government's exchange control regulation' may not permit him to pay the damages decreed against it or if it be a foreign company of unknown financial status or that the chances of any substantial damages being paid are questionable. The case of Thames Marshall (Export) Ltd vs Guinle 1977 Ch. 227 also supports Mr Khandaker's contention directly, while the decision in the ever important case of Beswick vs Beswick (1968 AC 58), supports him indirectly in that the House of Lords in that• case, which was primarily concerned with the doctrine of "Privity of Contract," also observed that if the common law award of damages is nominal and if multiplicity of legal actions are required to realise the claimed damages then the legal remedy of damages, even if available, will be deemed to be inadequate and the Equity will come forward in aid to grant specific performance "to do true justice to enforce the true contract that the parties have made, . to prevent the trouble and expenses of a multiplicity of action" (per Lord Upjohn). In this respect observation by Prof Alastair Hudson, in his book, "Principles of Equity and Trust," page 508, is worthy of perusing which reads, "The issue which arises then is as to the solvency of the respondent. It is all very well to say, 'let's not award an interlocutory injunction because damages would be sufficient remedy' if the respondent would not be able to pay the damages owed to the applicant. It is common practice, then, to require an undertaking to the ability to pay damages."

25. So, Mr Khandaker's argument is well ornamented full of substance and is in wholesome agreement with high authorities stemming from the birth place of the principles of Equity, and hence, in appropriate cases, injunction may, as Mr Khandaker submitted, be granted notwithstanding the fact that the nature of the loss is such that pecuniary award is enough to make good the loss if, of course, the plaintiff can show that the defendant does not have financial viability to satisfy a money decree, but again, as Prof. Hudson reckons, if the defendant fails to give a worthwhile undertaking about the sufficiency of this financial solvency. The present one however, is not an appropriate case for two reasons. Firstly, insofar as we are not swayed to hold that the plaintiff has been able to make out a prima facie case, we take it as "cadit quaestio," implying that the whole exercise of examining the question of irreparability of loss would be a futile one, particularly in view of Lord Diplock's observation in American Cynamid case which reads, "unless the material available to the Court at the hearing of the application for an interlocutory injunction fails to disclose that the plaintiff has any real prospect of succeeding in his claim for a permanent injunction at the trial, the court should go on to consider whether balance of convenience lies in favour of granting or refusing the interlocutory relief that is sought," (His Lordship also pointed out that, a significant factor in assessing the balance of convenience is the adequacy of damages to each party), and also in view of Pakistan Supreme Court's decision in the case of Mian Md Latifvs Province of We,st Pakistan [22 DLR (SC) 98J which reads: "It is needless to mention that in a case where temporary injunction is claimed, the plaintiff has only to make out that he has a good prima facie case meaning thereby that a serious question is to be tried in the suit and in the event of success if the injunction is not issued, he will suffer irreparable injury." (Surely implying that absence of prima facie will not necessitate consideration of any other factor). Secondly, the plaintiff/appellant has also not been able to, prima facie, establish that the defendant/respondent No. 1 does not have the financial ability to satisfy a possible decree against him. All that we can see in this respect is a sentence in the injunction petition which states, "As to the knowledge of the plaintiff, the defendant No.1 has no such asset within the jurisdiction," which is far from enough. We are rather inclined to hold that receipt of technical fee will elevate the defendant No. 1 's financial circumstances to make him more solvent to honour any possible decree. If, however, it transpires that the said defendant is trying to remove his money, the plaintiff will have a remedy under Order XXXVIII, rule 5, or by way of a Mareva Injunction.

26. In the light of our finding that, the plaintiff, on the basis of the material available before us, has failed to make out a prima facie case, we do not feel that there is any necessity to embark upon a detailed discussion on the balance of convenience either, (Balance of Justice in Donaldson MR's language (Francome vs Mirror Group of Newspapers Ltd 1984, 2 A11E.R 408, Attorney General vs Baker 1990, 3 All E.R 257) save making it clear that we have no hesitation to say, that the balance is tipped in favour of the defendant No. I. That said, however, we must. make it clear that our finding is based on prima facie evaluation of affidavit evidence only, which should not be misunderstood as a final finding on the substantive issues in the suit, which are to be determined by the learned trial judge, bearing in mind that, as the England's' Court of Appeal observed in the case of Fresh Fruit Wales Ltd vs Halbort, (Times, 29th January 1991) that the Court has jurisdiction to make, at an interlocutory stage, an order which may not be appropriate at the final trial and also by keeping in mind, as was observed by Lord Diplock, with whom other Lords of Appeal in Ordinary concurred in the case of American Cynamid vs Ethicon Ltd, that at the interlocutory stage it is no part of the Court's function to resolve conflicts of evidence on affidavit, which are matters to be dealt with at the trial.

27. Finally, we would reiterate another well-established principle of Equity which proclaims that an interlocutory injunction would not be granted if granting of the same amounts to infliction of disproportionate hardship on the defendant (Shell UK Ltd vs Lostock Garages Ltd. 1976 1WLR 1187). Hardship may be a factor in weighing the balance of convenience as well, but Bingham MR in Jaggard vs Saweyer (1995 1 WLR 269) pointed out that the test is one of oppression and the Court should not slide into application of a general balance of convenience test. In the present case, whatever may be the outcome of the suit, it would be oppressive to deprive the defendant No. 1 of the technical fee he, prima facie, seems to have earned from his UK- based principal, which he may invest for profit.

In view of the above, we find no reason to arrive at a finding different from the one arrived at by the learned Court below. Consequently, the appeal is dismissed and the connected Rule being Civil Rule No. 225 (FM) of 1998 is also discharged without any order as to cost.

End.
