full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam, J: The question raised in this rule is whether the opposite parties should seek their remedy by a suit or by an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure (hereinafter called the Code).

2. The relevant facts may be stated as follows: The predecessor-in-interest of the petitioner as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 4 of 1994 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka against the predecessor-in-interest of the present opposite parties and others impleding them as defendants praying for a decree of specific performance of contract alleging that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 entered into an agreement for sale with the predecessor-in-interest of the petitioner and while in pursuance of that agreement steps were being taken for transferring the suit land to the plaintiff. The, defendant No. 3 namely the predecessor in interest of the opposite parties purchased the suit land from the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 with full knowledge that the defend and Nos. 1 and 2 had earlier entered into an agreement with the plaintiff for sale of the suit property. It was thus averred that defendant No. 2 Mrs. Anowara Chowdhury, the predecessor-in-interest of the opposite parties being a purchaser with notice of the plaintiffs contract the contract is enforceable against her and hence the suit.

3. The defendant No. 3 the predecessor-in-interest of the opposite parties, contested the suit by filing a written statement denying he material allegations made in the plaint and asserted, inter alia, that a portion of the suit property has already been acquired by the Goventment and she denied any knowledge of the plaintiff's contract whatsoever. The case of the defendant No. 3 is that she is a bonafide purchaser for value without notice of the alleged contract. She also denied receipt of any letter and her signature and asserged that the suit is barred by limitation.

4. The suit was heard and tried by the learned Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka who after considering the evidence and materials on record decreed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 30.8.55. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree of the trial court the predecessor-in-interest of the opposite parties preferred First Appeal No. 205 of 1995 in the then High Court of Judicature in East Pakistan challenging the judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge. The said appeal was heard and disposed of by a Division Bench who after hearing the parties was pleased to allow the appeal in part and modified the decree of the trial court by their judgment and decree dated 22.3.1960. It appears that both the parties, that is, the plaintiff and the defendant No. 3 preferred two separate appeals before the Supreme Court and the appeal preferred by the defendant No. 3 was registered as Civil Appeal No. 30-D of 1961 and that of the plaintiff as Civil Appeal No. 31-D of 1961. The Supreme Court heard both the appeals analogously and disposed of the same by the judgment dated 17.3.64 whereby both the afore-said appeals were, dismissed and thereby affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the High Court.

5. It appears that in pursuance of the modified decree of the High Court the plaintiff did not take any step in aid for execution of the appellate decree till 9.8.93 and on 9.8.93 the heirs of the plaintiff filed an application under section 152, read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for drawing up a modified decree in the light of the judgment of the High Court dated 22.3.69 and the learned Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka, allowed that application and ordered for drawing up a modified decree in the light of the judgment of the High Court. It further appears that in pursuance of Order No. 56 dated 9.8.93 a modified decree was drawn by the learned Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka on 22.8.93.

6. Thereafter the petitioner filed Title Execution Case No. 21 of 1993 on 8.11.93 and the executing court after hearing the plaintiff decree holder on 20.11.93 directed the sheristadar to submit a report as regards the draft of the kabala on or before 26.11.93 and 25.11.93 the executing court approved the draft of the deed and it was executed and directed the sheristadar to register the deed in question and on the same day the deed was registered through Court. Thereafter on 30.11.93 the decree-holder filed an application for delivering possession of the suit land by partitioning the same and as such prayed for appointing an Advocate Commissioner and the said prayer was allowed and in due course the commission fee was deposited and on the application of the decree-holder the learned Advocate Commissioner was given the police force to execute the decree and the Advocate Commissioner affected partition of the suit land and handed over the possession to the decree holder and submitted his report on 5.11.95.

7. The grievance of the opposite parties is that the entire execution proceeding was started behind the back and without the know edging of the opposite parties and it is only on 2.11.95 they came to know of the proceedings of this execution case when the possession of the suit property was given to the petitioners by evicting the opposite parties from major portions of the suit property through the process of the court and on obtaining certified copies from the court came to know that the execution case was started on 6.11.95 without serving any notice upon them and practicing fraud upon the court the decree-holder grabed the suit property. The modified decree was drawn by the trial court on 22.8.93. Hence they filed application before the executing court under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the orders of the execution case and restoring session of the suit property to the petitioners.

8. It appears from the 151 application filed by the opposite parties that they have asserted therein that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 4 of 1955 by the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka, was merged and modified and part decree was passed in the First Appeal No. 205 of 1955 by the then High Court of Judicature of East Pakistan and the said part modified decree was drawn up as per provisions of Code of Civil Procedure, by the High Court on 28.4.1960 and the over all period of limitation of the aforesaid decree passed in First Appeal No. 205 of 1955 expired on 28.4.72 as per provisions of section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure. As no application for execution of the aforesaid decree passed in First Appeal No. 205 of 1955 was filed within three years of the decree as per Article 182 of the Limitation Act, so, legally the decree passed in First Appeal No. 205 of 1955 became time barred and died a natural death and was not at all enforceable in law. It further appears that in the meantime the defendant No. 3 that is, the predecessor-in-interest of the opposite parties died in 1987, leaving behind the opposite parties as her heirs and one Feroja Khatun, wife of the plaintiff, decree-holder of First Appeal No. 205 of 1955, instituted Title Suit No. 57 of 1992 in the Court of 4th Assistant Judge, Dhaka, against the petitioner impleading them as defendants for partition of the suit property claiming the same by way of gift from said M. Majid and the aforesaid suit on contest was dismissed on 12.4.93 on the finding that the decree passed in First Appeal No. 205 of 15 by the High Court is not enforceable, in la as the said decree was now executed as per law within the period of limitation as prescribed by Article 182 of the Limitation Act as well as provided by section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It further appears that the decree-holder filed an application on 9.8.93 in Title Suit No. 4 of 1955 in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka for drawing up a modified decree in the light of the judgment and order passed by the High Court in First Appeal No. 205 of 1955 and no notice was served on the opposite parties and that application was allowed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka vide his order dated 9.8.93. It is asserted by the opposite parties that the learned Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka, most illegally and without jurisdiction entertained and allowed the said application filed by the decree holder on 9.8.93 under section 151 read with section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure in as much as the decree passed by the trial court in Title Suit No. 5 of 1955 merged with the appellate decree passed by the High Court on 28.4.60 and in that view of the matter the learned Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka for drawing up a modified decree in the light of the judgment and order passed by the High Court in First Appeal No. 205 of 1995. It is further alleged that the decree-holder filed the Title Execution Case No. 21 of 1993 on 8.11.93 for executing the time barred decree by suppressing and withholding the said decree and without serving any notice upon the opposite parties as provided under Order 21, Rule 22(1Xb) of the Code of Civil Procedure as well as in violation of the provisions of Order 21 Rule 34 sub Rule (13) of the Code of Civil Procedure and the decree holder by pactising fraud upon the court obtained execution and registration of the sale deed on 28.11.93 through court behind the back and without any knowledge of the opposite parties. It is further asserted that the decree holder filed an application for partition of the suit property behind the back and without the knowledge of the opposite parties to make partition of the suit property although the executing court has no jurisdiction to partition the suit property in executing the decree for specific performance of contract. It is further alleged by the opposite parties that in order to further perpetuated the fraud evicted the opposite parties from major portions of the suit property on 2.11.95 through the process of the court by passing the process of this court and caused irreparable loss to the opposite parties by causing damage to the residential building of the opposite parties and evicted them from the portion of the suit land by practising fraud upon the court as well as on the opposite par-ties and thus the entire proceedings of the execution case were vitiated by palpable fraud,. practised upon the court.

9. The petitioner decree holder filed a written objection against the application wherein he has feried the material allegations made in the application and stated inter-alia that the decree passed by the  trial court was modified by the Supreme Court in Civil Appeal No. 30-D of 1961 and 31-D of 1961 preferred by the parties again at the judgment and modified decree of the High Court and they could not take any steps in aid for executing the decree modified by the High Court on the ground that the records of the case was sent down after a long delay. On top of that their original lawyer learned Advocate Golam Mostafa died in the meantime and the record of the case was misplaced and as such they could not take any step in the matter and as such they filed an application on 9.8.93 for modifying the decree of the trial court in the light, of the observations made by the High Court and as such within the period of limitation they have filed the execution case and it cannot be said that the execution case is barred by limitation. The further contention raised in the written objection is that the executing Court in the meantime executed the decree by partitioning the suit property and the sale deed in question has already been executed and registered through court and the possession of the suit property has also been handed over to the plaintiff decree-holder and as such the executing court has no jurisdiction to entertain the application filed by the opposite parties under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The further contention of the decree-holder is that rightly or wrongly after passing the execution order the executing court has become functus officio and as such had no jurisdiction to entertain the application filed by the defendant opposite parties.

10. The learned executing court after hearing the parties and on perusal of the records vide the impugned order No. 33 dated. 2.11.96 allowed the application filed by the opposite parties under section 151 of the Code and set-aside the entire proceedings of Title Execution Case No. 21 of 1993 and restored possession to the defendant opposite parties of the suit property, that is, status-quo ante was restored to the defendant opposite parties. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid order the decree-holder preferred this revisional application and obtained the instant rule. Mr. Abdul Hamid Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner urges 3 points before me. His first submission is that due to the death of the original lawyer of the plaintiff petitioner and due to unusual delay in getting back the records from the supreme court the petitioner could not file the execution case earlier and as soon as the record of the case was traceable the petitioner filed application on 9.8.93 before the learned Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka for drawing up a modified decree in the light of the observations given by the High Court Division in decreeing the appeal in part, namely First Appeal No. 205 of 1995 and the learned Subordinate Judge passed in order for drawing modified decree on 9.8.93 pursuant to which the modified decree was drawn on 22.8.93 and therefore the petitioner filed the Execution Case No. 21 of 1993 within one year from the date of drawing up the modified decree and as such no notice was required to be served on the defendant opposite parties as provided for by Order 21 Rule 22 of the Code. Mr. Chowdhury with much emphasis submitted that the instant application filed by the defendant opposite parties under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the entire proceedings of Title Execution Case No. 21 of 1993 is absolutely misconceived and not tenable in law inasmuch as proper remedy laid not in an application under section 151 of the Code but by way of a regular suit since there is an allegation of fraud levelled against the petitione. Mr. Chowdhury finally submits with much fore that in any view of the matter the executor  court after executing the decree became functus officio and as such had no jurisdiction whatsoever to entertain the application filed by the defendant opposite parties under section 151 of the Code.

11. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant opposite parties, on the other hand submits that the first submission made by Mr. Chowdhury is absolutely devoid of no substance and there is no provision in the Code to authorise the trial court to draw up a modified decree in the light of the observation given by the High Court and as such the application filed by the plaintiff petitioner on 9.8.93 for drawing up a modified decree in the light of the judgment and order passed by the High Court in First Appeal No. 2051 of 1995 is absolutely illegal and without jurisdiction and the plaintiff petitioner to get round the question of limitation has asserted so in this application and by practising fraud upon the court managed to get a modified decree drawn by the trial court on 22.8.93 which is absolutely illegal and without jurisdiction. The learned Advocate further submits that there was no necessity at all to draw up a modified decree by the trial court in as much as the decree passed by the trial court in Title Suit No. 4 of 1955 merged with the decree passed by the appellate court in Title Appeal No. 2051 of 1955. Thus, the learned Subordinate Judge labouring under misconception of law and mis-appreciation of facts most illegally and without jurisdiction drew up a modified decree on the application filed by the plaintiff petitioner under section 151 of the Code. Mr. Islam further submits that it is now well settled that if an order is obtained from a court by practising fraud upon the court the court is empowered to undo the wrong and pass a proper order of restitution by invoking its inherent jurisdiction under section 151 of the Code. The learned Advocate further submits that even in the absence of any fraud upon the court of it is found that a party to a suit by practising fraud on the court misled the court into passing on illegal order, the court has jurisdiction to rectify the mistake and pass necessary order to set it right and in fact it has so been done in the instant case. The learned Advocate further submits that when there is an allegation of fraud and if that allegation is established the concept of functus officio has no manner of application and the court is always entitled to invoke its jurisdiction under section 151 of the Code to set at right a wrong committed by it. In support of his contentions he relies on the decisions reported in AIR1985(SC)111, 1998 BLD(AD)121, 30DLR(SC)221, 43 DLR 207, 44DLR582, 31DLR108, 1998 BLD 318, AIR1977(SC) 1969 and AIR 1991(AP) 191.

12. On a perusal of the impugned order it appears that the learned executing court observed that whether by drawing up the modified decree on 9.8.93 the trial court has committed an error in law or not cannot be decided by the executing court and the executing court must confined to the legality and propriety of the executing order itself and thereafter the executing court finds that the plaintiff petitioner has got a decree for a 8 annas share of the suit property and it is apparent from the modified decree of the appellate court, that is the High Court that the decree-holder will get possession of the property after partitioning the property by metes and bounds but without filing any part it suit whatsoever got the suit property partitioned in the executing proceeding itself which is most illegal and without jurisdiction and hence found that executing court without jurisdiction and authority in law partitioned the suit property is executing the same. It further appears that the executing court also found that the plaintiff petitioner has not denied the fact that no notice of the execution proceeding was served on the defendant opposite parties. Thus found that no notice was at all served on the defendant opposite parties in respect of the execution case and thus found that the executing court most illegally evicted the defendant opposite parties from the suit land, with these findings the learned executing court found that the executing court most illegally and without jurisdiction entertained the execution case which is illegal and without jurisdiction and as such found that in the facts and circumstances of the instant case the application filed by the defendant opposite parties under section 151 of the Code is maintainable and thus set aside the entire proceedings of Title Execution Case No. 21 of 1993.

13. As to the first contention raised by Mr. Choudhury suffice it to say that on a query to the court he has frankly conceded that when a decree is modified by the appellate court the trial court has no authority in law to draw appear modified decree in the High of the appellate courts judgment and it not the requirement of law. Thus it is clear that it the reasons assigned by the plaintiff petitioner for approaching the learned Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka, as late as on 9.8.93 for drawing up a modified decree is absolutely illegal and without jurisdiction because it is now well settled proposition of law that if a decree of trial court is appealed against and in the appeal the decree is affirmed, recorded or modified by the appellate court then the decree passed by the trial court merges with the decree one the appellate court and there is no separate entity of any decree passed by the trial court. In that view of the matter it appears to me that the learned Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka, had no jurisdiction whatsoever to entertain the application filed by the plaintiff petitioner under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for drawing up a modified decree on 9.8.93. Thus, the order passed by the trial court on 9.8.93 is absolutely illegal and without jurisdiction and not tenable in law. In this connection I may refer back to the observation made by the executing court in the impugned order that whether the order dated 9.8.93 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka, is legal or not is not within the ambit of the execution case but suffice it to say that this court sitting in its revisional jurisdiction section 115 of the Code of is suo moto entitled to correct any illegality committed by the lower judiciary if it is brought to the notice of this Court. It appears from the record that the learned Subordinate Judge on an erroneous view Of law and facts at the instance of the plaintiff petitioner entertained the application filed by him under section 151 of the Code of which is absolutely illegal and without jurisdiction and that order dated 9.8.93 suffers from patent illegality and calls for interface in view of the fact that Article 182 of the Limitation Act provides a period of three years limitation for execution of a decree from the date of the decree and where that has been an appeal the date of final decree is the relevant date and in the instant case the final decree that is the appellate court has been drawn by the High Court on 28.4.60 and as such the plaintiff petitioner ought to have taken steps within the period of three years as contemplated by Article 182 and if the decree was kept alive by taking steps in aid then he could execute the same within 12 years from the date of the final decree was contemplated by section 48 of the Code but in the instant case it is apparent and admitted by all the parties that no such step was ever taken by the decree-holder within the period of limitation of three years and that is why to get round the question of limitation, it appears to me, that the plaintiff petitioner resorted to an application under section 151 of the Code on 9.8.93 and thus I find substance in the submission of Mr. Islam that only to get round the question of limitation and also to avoid the service of notice upon the defendant opposite parties of the execution case the plaintiff petitioner has resorted to that method.

14. The second contention of Mr. Chowdhury is that the defendant opposite parties have filed the application for setting aside the entire proceeding of execution case on the ground of fraud committed by the plaintiff petitioner on the court and in that view of the matter since the executing court has already executed the decree the proper remedy lies in a separate suit and the application filed by the defendant opposite parties Under section 151 of the Code was misconceived and not tenable in law and the learned executing court erroneously entertained the same. This submission is also absolutely misconceived and devoid of any substance. It is now well settled that if fraud is committed upon the court by a party the court is entitled to invoke its jurisdiction under section 151 of the Code. In this connection it may be said that the Calcutta High Court went to the en-tent of saying that not only has the court power, but it is the duty, to set aside a decree obtained by fraud practiced upon the court, when appraised of it, see 19 CWN 419. There is a long line of decisions out of which some of the decisions have been cited by Mr. Mahmudul Islam wherein it has been consistently held by this Division as well as the Appellate. Division that if fraud is committed upon the court the court is always entitled to set it right by invoking its jurisdiction under section 151 of the Code because fraud vitiaties everything and an innocent party cannot be allowed to suffer for the fraud committed by the other party and a court of law can never give any latitude to a party who committed the fraud. The decisions relied on by Mr. Islam show that the court preserves its inherent jurisdiction to set at naught any illegality committed by it either due to misapprehension of fact and or ignorance of law and fraud committed on it by a party. In this case it may be mentioned that although Mr. Chowdhury submits that the application filed by the defendant opposite parties under section 151 is not maintainable but he failed to lay his hands on any decision of this court of any other jurisdiction. On the other hand the preponderance of decisions is that when a fraud is committed upon a court the court is entitled to invoke its inherent jurisdiction and the other remedy available to the aggrieved party is not answer to the question. It has been decided in the case reported in 31DLR109 that if fraud has been committed upon the party as a result of which the court has been misled into passing certain orders then it is a fraud upon the court and in such case the court is entitled under its inherent powers to set aside any order passed upon a false representation. The court had inherent power to correct its own proceedings when it has been misled into passing an order by the fraud of any party to the suit. The other remedy by way of a suit involving delay and expenses cannot be deemed to be an alternative remedy when the same relief can be obtained under section 151 of the Code with less delay and expenses. In the similar line there is a decision reported In AIR 1991 (AP) 191 wherein it has been held that a tribunal can under inherent power rectify injustice brought out by its own order. Our Appellate Division in the case reported in 30 DLR(SC)221 has held that the court has an inherent power under section 151 of the Code so set aside its order passed under a misapprehension of facts when true facts are brought to light and that the court has also power under the aforesaid section 151 of the Code to vacate an order obtained by misleading the court and practising fraud upon it and the same view is reiterated in the decision reported in 44 DLR 552 wherein it has been held that in case of fraud upon the cow it may exercise inherent powers to set this right even rough are alternative remedies open. The Indian Supreme Court in the case reported in AIR1977(SC) 1569 went one step further and observed that every tribunal has the inherent power to prevent its machinery from being made a sham, thereby reversing down the rule of law itself as an object of public redicale. It will and must preserve any statagem self-defeating if a party indulges in making the low the laughing atock, for, the court will call him to order. Similar view was earlier expressed by this Division in the case reported in 40 DLR 239 wherein it has been held that willful concealment of a material fact on the part of the petitioners which tantamount to practising fraud upon court is a sufficient ground to invoke the provision of section 151 of the Code to set at naught the ex-parte decree, even though there is alternative remedy provided in the Code for setting aside ex-parte decree. In this connection I may refer to the observations made by the Supreme Court in the case reported in 30 DLR(SC)221 wherein in the course of the judgment Ashanuddin Chowdhury, J who delivered the judgment has stated in the following terms:

In view of the facts and circumstances of the case, even if there were an alternative remedy, it would not bar the exercise of power under section 151 of the Code by the court section 151 preserves the inherent power of the Court to make such order as may be necessary for the ends of justice. It may be noted that the provisions of the Code are generally meant to serve the ends of justice by the very nature they cannot read all possible circumstances. Consequently every court has are inherent owner to make an order it considers necessary for the ends of justice. It thus appears that the second contention raised by Mr. Chowdhury is absolutely misconceived and not tenable in law.

<u>15. Now the final question that calls for determination is whether the executing court was competent to entertain the application filed by the opposite parties under section 151 of the Code in view of the fact and circumstances of the case particularly when the executing proceeding came to an end and the executing court is not in siesin of the matter. The same sort of contention was raised in the case resorted in 44DLR552 and a single Bench of this court held that in cases of fraud upon the court, it may exercise inherent powers to set things right even though there are alternative remedies open. In the case of Baidyanth Dubey Vs. Deobands Sing, 1968 SCD 274, the Supreme Court of India held that a court has inherent powers to recall orders obtained by practicing fraud on it, at the instance of a party to the proceedings and there is no question of the court being functus officio. A party cannot be allowed to take advantage of its own wrong and fraud vitiates everything. Besides the court always preserves its inherent powers to set at naught any illegality committed by it.</u>

16. It is thus clearly established beyond any doubt that in cases of fraud upon the court, the court any exercise its inherent powers to set things right even though there are alternative remedies open. In some of the cases it has been observed that not only the court has such powers but it is its duty to set aside the decree or order obtained by fraud practiced upon the court itself when apprised of it.

<u>17. On a perusal of the impugned order it appears that the learned executing court set aside the entire proceedings of Title Execution Case No. 21 of 1993 on the ground that the executing court acted beyond its jurisdiction but did not give any finding as to whether any fraud was committed by the plaintiff petitioner upon the court and did not advert to that point on the ground that it is beyond the scope of the instant case to enter into the correctness or otherwise of the order dated 9.9.93 passed by the trial court but I have already found that it is absolutely illegal and without jurisdiction. Besides, suffice it to say that if the ultimate order is sustainable in law the reasons assigned by the court then become irrelevant or is of little significance. There are decisions of this court as well as of the High Court Division that if on a scrutiny of the reworks it is found that the order passed by the Court is ultimately supportable in law but the reasons assignees for passing such an order is not tenable that will have no bearing upon the merits of the order so passed because on an ultimate analysis of the facts and circumstances of the case it is found that the order passed by the court is in accordance with law. In the instance case the learned Executing Court on three ground set aside the entire proceedings of the Execution. Case No. 2 of 1993. Those grounds no doubt are valid grounds in view of the facts and circumstances of the case. These are sufficient to sustain the impugned order as a valid order in the eye of law but it appears to me that on top of that it must be added that the plaintiff petitioner with an ulterior motive and to get round the question of limitation and to mislead the trial court filed an application on 9.8.91 under section 151 read with section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure for drawing up of a modified which is palpably wrong and erroneous. Since the foundation of the present execution case is based on fraudulent act of the plaintiff petitioner the impugned order its also sustainable in that view of the fact that by committing a fraud upon the trial court the plaintiff petitioner had managed to get an order in his favour on 9.8.93 and pursuant to that a modified decree was drawn on 22.8.92. The practice adopted by the plaintiff petitioner must by deprecated and that fraud is committed on the court is apparent from the order dated 9.8.93 wherein it has been observed by the learned trial court that"</u>

<u>“নথি পর্যালোচনা করিলাম। নখি পর্যালোচনায় দেখা যায় যে মহামান্য হইকোর্ট ও সুপ্রীম ও কোর্টের রায়েরে কপি ১৯৬৮ ইং সাল হইতে আপীল আছে কিন্তু নথিতে সেই মর্মে কোন লিপি হয় নাই।</u>

<u>Thus it is apparent from the Order No. 56 dated 9.8.93 that the copies of the decree and order passed by the High Court and the Supreme Court were already with the records of the case and the assertion made by the plaintiff petitioner that they did not file any application prior to that date due to non-availability of the record of the Supreme Court appears to be baseless. In this connection it may be mentioned that Mr. Chowdhury also frankly conceded that the records of trial court is not at all necessary in initiating an executing proceeding under Order 21 because simply the certified copy of the judgment and decree sought to be executed is to be supplied along with the application for execution of the decree. Thus, it appears to me that the fraud is apparent on the face of the record, in any view of the matter, I am of the opinion that the application filed by the plaintiff-petitioner on 9.8.93 under section 151 of the code was not at all maintainable.</u>

18. I have gone through the entire records the execution case and on a perusal of the same it appears that in filing the execution are the plaintiff petitioner has miserably railed to comply with the provision of Order 21 Rule 22(1)(b) of the Code of Civil Procedure as well as the provisions of Order 21 Rule 34(2)(3) of the Code and on that ground also the execution proceeding is not at all maintainable and the plaintiff petitioner by suppressing the facts and misleading the executing court managed to get the execution proceeding started and got the decree executed by fraudulent means. Thus I do not find any substance in this revisional application.

19. In the result, the Rule is discharged with a cost of Tk. 5,000/- to be paid by the petitioner to the defendant-opposite parties within 30 days from the date of receipt of this order by the trial court.

The order of stay granted earlier by this court is hereby vacated.

End.

Mr. A.K.M. Nazrul Islam with Mrs. Purabi Rani Saha, Advocate ----- for petitioners.

parties:
Md. Gias Uddin and others
Vs.
Md. Nowab Ali & others
full_judgment:
Md. Tafazzul Islam, J: This Rule is directed against the judgment and decree dated 17.11.98 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Jamalpur, in Title Appeal No. 132 of 1997 allowing the appeal and setting aside the judgment and decree dated 30.10.97 passed by the Court of Assistant Judge, Melandah, Jamalpur, Sadar in Other Suit No. 4 of 1995.

2. Brief fact are that the opposite party Nos. 1, 2 and 3, as plaintiffs, instituted the above Other Suit No. 4 of 1995 praying for declaration of their joint right, title and interest in the suit plot stating inter alia that 1.781/2 acres of land under C.S. Khatian No. 94 and R.O.R. Khatian No. 191 Mauza Chardaga, P.S. Melandah, District Jamalpur, belonged to Baben Sheikh (IV 82). Gol Mamud (IV 82) and Rahmat Ali (V.02) and Gol Mahmud died leaving Nawab Ali the plaintiff No. 1, Tayab Ali, Rahmat Ali, the defendant No. 5 Baban Ali died leaving behind his son Jaban Ali and daughters gendy, Jamury and wife Rupjan Beoya, Rupjan Beoya gifted her share i.e. 54 ½ decimals of land to Samsul Haque, Jamury died leaving behind his son Velu, defendant No. 3, Gendy transferred 90 decimals of land to Jaban Ali by registered Sale deed Gul Mahmud during his life time sold 90 decimals of land to Jaban Ali. Thus Jaban Ali became owner of 3.73 acres of land out of which he sold 28 decimals of land to Meen, Gias, Reza and Maruddin and at the time of possessing and enjoining the balance 3.45 acres of land the aforesaid, Jaban Ali died leaving behind his 3 sons Bisu, Gafur and Gias the defendant No. 1, daughters Urmeli the plaintiff No. 2, Kholeli the plaintiff No. 3 and wife Jariman, Bisu and Gafur died an bachelor teaming behind mother Jariman brother, Gias defendant No. 1, and sister Urmeli and Koheli, i.e. plaintiff Nos. 2-3 Jariman gifted her 52 decimals of land to plaintiff Nos. 2-3 by registered deed of hiba Jariman Ali died leaving behind his son defendant No. 1 and two daughters plaintiff Nos. 2-3. Then three brothers Bisu, Gafur and Gias and the plaintiff Nos. 2-3, by family partition obtained 43 decimals of land from Dag No. 31.7 ½  decimals of land from Dag No. 136, 79 decimals of land from Dag No. 174 and 43 decimals of land from Dag No. 176. There Gias, the defendant No. 1 them sold 1234 decimals of land to plaintiff No. 1 and the defendant No. 5 by registered deed No. 17610 dated 26.12.70. The plaintiff No. 2 transferred 50 decimals of land to the plaintiff No. 1 by registered deed No. 447 dated 13.1.88 and thus the plaintiffs are possessing and enjoining 1.78 decimals of land but during R.O.R. operation, the name of the plaintiffs No. 2 and 3 were excluded and the suit land was wrongly recorded in the name of defendant No. 1 and his mother Jariman and hence plaintiffs instituted the instant suit.

3. The defendant Nos. 1 and 4-10 contested the suit and filed written statements controverting the title, right and interest of the plaintiffs on all maierial points. They however admitted the possession of the plaintiff in a portion of the suit land but their contention is that the heirs of C.S. tenant Rahmat Ali and all the heirs of Gul Mahmud were not made party in the suit and heirs of Mearuddin Sarker and others were not also made party in the suit and so the suit is bad for defect of parties and during R.O.R. operation the name of Giasuddin and other heirs were correctly recorded and Nowab All could not get possession on the basis of purchase deed from Khulai and Urmelu and that the plaintiff nos. 2 and 3 never appeared in court and by forging their thumb-print the plaintiff No. 1 instituted the instant suit and the plaintiff having not prayed the relief of partition, the suit is not maintainable.

4. The learned trial court found that under the provisions of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, the plaintiff cannot get a decree of declaration in respect of joint property owned by the plaintiffs and defendants and the plaintiffs ought to have filed a suit for partition and as such the suit is not maintainable and further the suit is also bad for defect of parties. The learned appellate court by the impugned judgment and decree allowed the appeal holding that the plaintiffs appellants were entitled to joint declaration of their title in the suit land and so the suit in maintainable and further, the plaintiffs appellants and defendants-respondents may pray for their respective saham by filing a partition suit. Accordingly, the judgment and decree of the trial court was set aside.

5. Mr. A.K.M. Nazrul Islam, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, relying on the case of Enjaheruddin Miah alias Md. Enjaharuddin Vs. Mohammad Hossain and others reported in 18 BLD(AD)3, the case of Narayan Sarker Vs. Siraj Miah reported in 1989 BLD(AD)9, in the case of Paran and others reported in AIR 137 (Rangun) 427 and the case of Kaup Nath Singh vs. Lala Ram Din Lal reported in ILR 15 Calcutta, 117, submits that the reliefs sought by the plaintiff in the suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and the plaintiffs ought to have prayed for partition and the appellate Court considering the need of partition suit, at the and of his judgment, held that after declaration of joint title the plaintiffs and the defendants may file partition suit praying their respective saham. Mr. Islam lastly submits that the suit is also liable for dismissed for defect of parties.

6. Mr. M. Enayetur Rahim, the learned Advocate for the opposite party Nos. 1-3, submits that since the title and possession of the plaintiffs having been admitted by the defendants, no consequential relief is necessary at all in the present suit and in the present suit the cause of action arose merely because record of right of the suit was wrongly recorded in the name of the defendant No. 1 and as it evident from the deposition, after the death of their mother Jarimunnessa the defendant No. 1. Giasuddin, being her son and the plaintiffs No. 2 and 3 i.e. Urmali and Kholai, daughters, being her heirs, acquired title and interest in the suit land and they were also in possession of the suit land Mr. Rahim next relying on the case of Shankar Chandra Das Vs. Kala Chand Das reported in 46 D.L.R. 419, the case of Joy Narayan Vs. Shree Nanta reported in AIR 1922 Calcutta, 8, submits that the question of partition arises, when after request, the other co-sharer refuses to give saham but in present case, there being no such refusal, the cause of action for further relief of partition did not arise. Mr. Rahim lastly submits that the suit is also not bad for defect of parties as all the persons whose names were recorded in the record of right were made defendants.

7. Heard the learned advocates:

As it appears the learned trial court apart from holding that the plaintiffs in the present case did not pray for partition, also house that since all the persons showed as owners of C.S. Khatian No. 94 and or thus successors, were not made parties, the suit is also bad for defect of parties and further since the plaintiffs on one hand claimed that they are owners of land situated in C.S. Khatian No. 94, but by subsequent amendment deleted C.S. Khatian No. 94 from the plaint and so the plaintiffs also did not come with clean hand. The trial court having found that D.W.1 in his deposition stated that the area of the suit land is 1.781/2 decimal of lands but in the amended plaint he showed the area of the suit land as 3.45 acres of land and that Ext. 5 i.e. Deed No. 2418 dated 1.4.58 shows that from C.S. Khatian No. 95 land has been transferred whereas the suit Khatian is 94 and thus in spite of repeated amendment the plaintiffs could not show what is their actual claim and so dismissed the suit holding as follows:

উভয় পক্ষের মন্তব্য এবং সাক্ষ্য প্রমানাদী পর্যালোচনা ক্রমে প্রতীয়মান হয় যে বাদীপক্ষ তাহাদের মোকদ্দমা প্রতিকার পাইতে পারে না।

As it appears, the learned Assistant Judge did not at all discuss the evidence of parties while arriving at the aforesaid finding.

8. The  learned Appellate Court, found that the predecessor of the plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 and the contesting defendant No. 1 were admittedly the owner of the suit land and the defendant No. 1 and the plaintiff No. 1 purchased some portion of the suit land from the plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 and that the plaintiff Nos. 1-3 are owners in possession of the suit land and since in the record of right, only the name of the defendant No. 1 was recorded Propping name of defendant Nos. 2 and 3 and also other co-owners in possession, the plaintiffs brought the present suit and the appellate court found that the defendant No. 1 who deposed as D.W. No. 1, and also the D.Ws 4-5 admitted that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land jointly with the defendants and the plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 are co-owners and D.W.1 also categorically stated that it is at the instance of his uncle that during the recording of record of right the name of the plaintiff Nos. and 3 were not included and D.W.5 also stated that both plaintiffs and the defendants are in possession of the suit land and defendant No. 1 in his deposition stated that the sisters i.e. the plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 were not given any saham after partition and the joint title and possession of the plaintiffs and the defendants having not been denied, the present suit was maintainable.

9. Regarding defect of parties, the appellate court held that the plaintiff did not challenge the C.S. Khatian and they are aggrieved due to wrong recording of record of right and the appellate court found that all the persons in whose name the record of right was prepared, were made defendants and in view of the above, the appellate court, held that the suit is not bad for defect of parties.

10. It further appears the learned trial court did not give any finding at all regarding title and possession of the plaintiffs as well as the defendants in the suit land and in a very short out manner passed the judgment and decree but the appellate court considering the evidence of both the parties found that the plaintiffs owners of the suit land along with the defendant No. 1 an co-owner and the appellate court, on the basis of the evidence of D.Ws 7, 4, and 5 also found that the plaintiffs are in joint possession of the suit land.

11. I also found that since the names of all the person recorded in the record of right have been made, defendants the suit is not bad for defect of parties.

12. The only question which is left for decease is whether suit is maintainable without any further prayer for partition From the contents of paragraph 7 of the decision reported in 18 BLD (AD) 77 cited by Mr. Islam, it appears that in the said decision the plaintiffs in their plaint, did not make any specific assertion to the effect that they have inherited specific plot of land from their father and the plaintiffs in the said decision did not also led evidence to the above affect whereas in the present suit, facts are different in as such as in the present case plaintiffs No. 2 and 3 made specific assertion to the plaint that they have inherited the suit plot from their father and the plaintiff No. 1 also claimed that they purchased some portion of the suit plot from the plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3. Accordingly, the facts being different, the principles as laid down in 18 BLD (AD) 77 and not applicable in the present case. In the decision reported in 1989 BLD (AD) 9 cited by Mr. Islam, the plaintiffs sought for declaration that vested property case started in the year 1979 for declaring the suit land as an enemy and vested property, is illegal and void and in the plaint the plaintiffs claimed out of 1/3 share of the suit land but and from the contents of the plaint it could not be ascertained what was the share of the other co-owners in the suit land and it was not clear whether 1/3rd share of the suit land, representing the original owner, has been included in the vested property case but the facts of the present case are completely different and so the principle laid down in the above decision to the effect that the plaintiffs in the aforesaid facts and circumstances caught to have filed the suit for partition is not at all applicable in the present case. Likewise the fats of decisions AIR 1937 (Rangun), 427 and ILR15, (Calcutta), 117 being completely different, the principle laid down in the above decisions are also not applicable in the present case.

The case of the petitioners is that the plaintiffs could have sought further relief by way of partition then that of a mere declaration of title and the omission to pray of partition makes the suit liable to be dismissed. However, as it appears, the legislature in section 42 of the "specific Relief Act, used the word further relief' and not the word "other relief'. In view of the expression "further relief' and this further relief must consequently relief in relation to the legal character or right as to property which the plaintiff is entitled to and whose title to such character or right the defendant denies or he is interested in denying and it must also be relief appropriate to and necessarily consequent on the right of title asserted. So a declaratory decree in not to be dismissed on the ground that it is barred by the provision to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, unless it quite cleared that the plaintiff ought to seek further relief which he has failed to claim although such relief flows directly and necessarily from declaration sought for, as pet example when a person is out of possession of the land in respect of which he seeks to have title declared, possession of the land in dispute is further consequential relief appropriate to the declaration prayed for an should as a general Rule be sought because unless the same is done and if the plaintiff were allowed to seek the full measure of relief, viz first on declaration of title in a suit  for declaratory relief and next, ejectment in a suit for recovery of possession of it would led to multiplicity of litigation.

14. But as it appears in the present case the position is different as the plaintiffs are in joint possession of a joint property to the extent of the share claimed by them and they asked for the declaratory relief because of the wrong recording of the record of right and in case of such a suit, it is difficult to appreciate on which principle the plaintiff should be driven to seek for partition as a consequential relief.

15. One of the incidence of joint property is that it may be enjoyed jointly; another incident is that the joint character is laible to be terminated. If a co-owner is continued to enjoy joint property as such, there is no reason why he should be driven to seek for partition, merely because cloud has arisen on that title because of wrong recording of record of right. 16. Of course the provision of section 42 forbids a suit for pure declaration without further relief but it does not compel the plaintiff to sue for all the relief which could possibly be granted or debar him from obtaining a relief which he wants unless at the same time he seeks for a relief which he does not want. It may be that the plaintiff requires nothing more than a mere declaration and in those circumstances to refuse to made the decree asked for, will be a denial of justice. Accordingly since cloud has arisen on the title of the plaintiff because of wrong recording of ROR, a declaration of title which all that the plaintiff need.

17. In 46 DLR 419 cited by Mr. Lahi the High Court Division also held that in a case of original ownership the plaintiffs and defendant being in joint possession of the suit property, suit for declaratory relief in respect of the share of the plaintiff in a specified land without seeking partition is maintainable.

<u>18. Accordingly since the plaintiffs are in joint possession of the immovable property, they are entitled to a suit praying for declaratory relief only with a view to remove a cloud on their title created due to wrong recording of ROR, because in such a suit, declaration of title is all that the plaintiff needs and so they are not called upon to ask for consequential relief by way of partition.</u>

<u>In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order to cost.</u>

End.

lawyer:

Brexco Bremer Export Contor Brand-Defendants ------ Appellants
Vs.
M/s. Popular Biscuit Limited ------ Plaintiff-respondent
full_judgment:
Md Mamtazuddin Ahmed, J: This appeal has been filed by the defendant Nos. 3 to 6 against the order dated 25.5.1993 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge in Money Suit No. 1 of 1992 refusing to stay the proceedings of the suit instituted by the plaintiff, claiming a decree for Tk. 89,20,459.30 being compensation for late Erection, Erection costs, wrong shipment, supply of under capacity machineries, over consumption of electricity and short shipments and as detailed in the plaint.

2. It appears from the plaint that the plaintiff floated International Press Tender on 23.12.1983 inviting offers from bonafide suppliers and manufactures for supplying for brand new machinery and equipment’s for soft Biscuit manufacturing factory. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 on 16.1.1984 submitted tender through defendant No. 3 and others and the tender was accepted by the plaintiff and they entered into a contract on 2.5.1984 with the plaintiff for supplying of machineries, equipment’s and services and also for supervision, erection and installation of the same at project site but the defendants did not act as per terms of the contract rather they violated the terms of the contract utterly. In view of arbitration clause of the contract the plaintiff on 28.10.1987 filed Arbitration Case before the International Chamber of Commerce (hereinafter referred to as I.C.C) at Paris, France, against the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 but the arbitration was ultimately failed as the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 raised a new plea on 5.8.1988 to deposit security of D.M. 25,000/-as Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangtha invoked the performance guarantee as a counter claim which is to be adjusted before the arbitration proceeding is started I.C.C. ultimately informed the plaintiff and the defendants by its letter dated 14.2.1991 that in the event, the claims are considered withdrawn without prejudice to the parties and in the facts and circumstances of the case, arbitration could not be proceeded. The plaintiff then constrained to file the present suit for realisation of the amount on several counts, which has been stated in the plaint.

3. The defendant Nos. 3 to 6 having received the summons entered appearance before the Subordinate Judge on 25.4.1992 and applied for time for tiling written statements the content of which are quoted hereunder:

“নিবেদন এই যে,

অত্র মোকদ্দমায় অদ্য সমনজারী হইয়া ফেরত আসা এবং তাহা নথি সামিলের জন্য আছে। ১নং বিবাদী একটি জার্মানী কোম্পানী। ১নং বিবাদীর অফিস জার্মানীর গ্রাজবার্গে অবস্থিত। বাংলাদেশে ১নং বিবাদীর কোন অফিস বা কর্মস্থল নাই। বাদীপক্ষ তঞ্চকতাপূর্বক ১নং বিবাদীর অফিস ঢাকাতে দেখাইয়াছে। মূলতঃ ১নং বিবাদীর উপর কোন প্রসেস আইনতঃ ইস্যু হয় নাই। জারীও হয় নাই। বাদীপক্ষ ১নং বিবাদীর সঠিক ঠিকানা দিতে বাধ্য। এই ওকালতনামা দিয়া হাজির হইয়াছে। এই বিবাদীপক্ষে বর্ণনা দেওয়ার জন্য প্রয়োজনীয় কাগজপত্র জোগাড় করা আবশ্যক। তদবস্থায় এই বিবাদীপক্ষে বর্ণনা দানের জন্য ২ (দু্ই) মাস সময় দেওয়ার প্রয়োজন নতুবা এই বিবাদীপক্ষের অপূরনীয় ক্ষতির কারণ হইবে।

অতএব, ২-৬ নং বিবাদীগণ পক্ষে বিনীত প্রার্থনা হুজুর আদালত দায় প্রকাশে উপরোক্ত অবস্থাধীনে অত্র মোকদ্দমায় এই বিবাদীপক্ষের বর্ণনা দানের জন্য ২ (দুই) মাস সময় দানের মর্জি হয়।”

The defendants, then submitted applications on 27.5.1992 and 16.6.1992 on the similar averments for filing written statements, Defendants submitted another application on 16.6.1992 under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for supplying the plaint in Bengali Language as the plaint was filed in English Language.

4. Finally, the defendants submitted another application under section 34 of the Arbitration Act on 17.8.1992 stating, inter alia, that Article 18(1) and 18(2) of the contract clearly stipulated that arbitration has to be held in Dhaka which has not yet been held as per said Articles and on such averments they prayed for staying the proceeding of the suit.

5. The plaintiff submitted written objection on 26.9.1992 against the aforesaid application under section 34 of the Arbitration Act denying the allegations made in the application and stated further that the application under section 34 of the Arbitration Act is not maintainable as the defendants filed application for time for tiling written statements. Moreover these defendants have not stated in the application that they are still ready and willing to decide matter by arbitration and to do all things necessary for proper conduct of the arbitration and as such the petition is liable to be rejected.

6. The learned Subordinate Judge after hearing the parties by his order dated 25.5.1993 rejected the application under section 34 of the Arbitration Act holding that arbitration could not be concluded due to the unamenable conduct of the defendants and the record does not show that the defendants participated in the said arbitration and their conduct appears to be malafide one.

7. Mr Ozair Farooq appearing on behalf of the defendant-appellants has taken us to the agreement, applications for time as well as application under section 151 of the Code Civil Procedure for supplying copy of the plaint in 'Bangle Language counter-affidavit, affidavit-in-reply and annexures thereto. Mr. Ozair Farooq also placed the application under section 34 of the Arbitration Act and the written objection filed by the plaintiff-respondent and other materials on record. The learned Advocate for the appellants made two fold submissions in as much as the present defendant-appellants were mere commission agent and signed the contract having been authorised by the principal defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and the period of said letter of authority expired on 31.12.1985 and as such these defendants are neither necessary nor proper party to the suit and considering that aspect of the case these defendants were not make parties before the I.C.C. at Paris. Therefore, the defendants have no liabilities but they are made parties in the suit with malafide motive and the address of the defendant No.1 was given at 5 Bangahondhu Avenue, Dhaka with ulteriar motive. His next submission is that Article 18(1) and Article 18(2) of the contract speak for holding arbitration at Dhaka and without resorting to hold such arbitration at Dhaka the suit cannot be proceeded with. He again submits that the applications seeking time for filing written statements cannot be construed as steps in the proceeding as contemplated under section 34 of the Arbitration Act as the defendants could not understand the contents of the plaint for not being supplied with the plaint in "Bangla' language and that submission of application was not unconditional which will be evident from the averments of the application dated 27.4.1992 and such conduct does not amount "to taking any other steps in the proceedings". The learned Advocate further submits that the learned Subordinate Judge erred in law in rejecting the application under section 34 of the Arbitration Act in not finding in that these defendants were not made parties before the I.C.C. and also the fact that the plaint in "Bangla' language was not supplied before 17.8.1992. In support of his contention Mr. Ozair Farooq referred to certain decisions such as in the cases of Nuruddin Abdulhussain versus Abu Ahmed Abdul Jalli, AIR 1950 (Bom) 127; Food Corporation of India and another versus Yadav Engineer and Contractor, Supreme Court Cases 1982 (2SCC) 499; Badsha Miah Sowdagar versus Nurul Haque and others 18DLR 237; Sea Liberties Inc. versus The Province of East Pakistan and others 19 DLR376; Md. Esack versus Raja Miah and others, 20 DLR 1120; Pioneer Rope Manufacturing Co. Ltd. and others versus Pakistan Industrial Credit and Invest Corporation Ltd. and others, 21 DLR554.

8. In reply to the submissions of the learned Advocate for the defendant-appellants, Mr. Azizul Haque, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-respondent submits that the learned Subordinate Judge committed no error of law in rejecting the application under section 34 of the Arbitration Act holding that the arbitration held at Paris before the ICC could not be proceeded with as the defendants raised a new plea for depositing D.M. 25,000/- as security by the plaintiff subject to the adjustment before the arbitration is taken place. The learned Advocate further submits that the defendants filed several applications for time for filing written statements which is definitely a step in the proceeding. Illustrating his argument Mr. Aziz again submits that the appellants nowhere in the application under section 34 of the Arbitration Act stated that the defendants are still remain ready and willing to do all things necessary to the proper conduct of the arbitration and hence the defendants are not entitled to get order of staying the proceedings of the suit. In support of his submission he placed some decisions held in the cases of Secretary of the State and another versus Surendra Mohan Lahiri and another, AIR 1939 (Patna) 118; W. Weed and sons Ltd. versus Bengal Corporation and another; AIR 1956 (Cal) 238, Union of India versus Hans Raj Gupta and Co. AIR 1957 (Allahabad) 91; The State of Uttar Pradesh and another versus M/s Janki Saran Kailash Chandra and another, AIR 1973 (SC) 2071; Muhammad Idris and others versus Tobarak Hossain; 17DLR (1965)209. But those decisions are not applicable under the facts and circumstances of the present case.259.

9. In order to arrive at a decision about contentions made by the learned counsels of the parties on the question of staying of the proceedings of the suit, we may refer to definition of the clause and other relevant Articles of the contract which run as follows:-

"Article-1- Definitions: "The "Seller" shall mean and include M/s. Brexco Smbh. Bredenstra 11, Breman, West Germany and/or its successors-in interest: Legal representatives and assigns and the Local agent. "Local Agent" shall mean and include M/s. Burhan (Bangladesh) Ltd. and/or its successors-in-interest legal representative and assigns".

"Article-18: Arbitration :

18, -1. In case of dispute or difference between the contracting parties arising out of this contract relating to any technical matter, the parties agree to refer the matter to a committee of three technical experts. The Buyer, the written approval of the BSRS, and the Seller shall appoint one expert each and the two experts so nominated shall, by common agreement appoint the third.

18,-2. Any dispute or difference arising out of this contract may be mutually settled and in case fails by arbitration in accordance with the rules of the Conciliation and Arbitration of the International Chamber of Commerce, Paris, by one or more Arbitrator's as may be appointed by them. The arbitration shall be held at Dhaka.

" The material question falls before us for adjudication as to whether the defendant-appellants after submission of applications for filing written statements are entitled to the advantage provided in section 34 of the Arbitration Act. Section 34 of the Arbitration Act runs as follows:

"Sec.34. Power to stay legal proceedings where there is an arbitration agreement. Where any party to an arbitration agreement or any person claiming under him commences any legal proceedings against any other party to the agreement or any person claiming under him in respect of any matter agreed to be referred, any party to such legal proceedings may, at any time before filing a written statement or taking any other steps in the proceedings, apply to the judicial authority before which the proceedings, are pending to stay the proceedings; and if satisfied that there is no sufficient reason why the matter should not be referred in accordance with arbitration agreement and that the applicant was, at the time when the proceeding were commenced, and still remains, ready and willing to do all things necessary to the proper conduct of the arbitration, such authority may make an order staying the proceedings."

10. It thus appears that the prayer for the stay under section 34 of the Arbitration Act must be made before filing written statements or before taking any steps in the proceedings. It is true that if it appears that without weaving one's right under the agreement for arbitration some steps are taken for the purpose of the application of the nature of the present case then the defendants will be free to make an unqualified prayer for stay interns of section 34 of the Arbitration Act. But if it appears that he/they have taken some steps in the proceedings signifying thereby his/their submission to the jurisdiction of the Court then certainly it is to be deemed to have waived their right in the Arbitration Clause and it should be deemed also to have acquisance in the proceeding before the Court. In the present case we have found that the plain-tiff did not implead the defendant No. 3 in the arbitration proceeding before the I.C.C. at Paris, France though the agreement shows that the 'Seller' shall mean and include "M/s. Bresco Gmbh Bredenstre II, Bremen, West Germany and/or its successors in interest legal representatives and assigns and the Local Agent and that "Local Agent" shall mean and include M/s. Burhan (Bangladesh) Ltd. and/or its successors-in-interest legal representatives and assigns. "The defendant No. 3 was the local agent of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2. As a result it cannot be said that the present defendant-appellants before us were not given opportunity to contest in the arbitration proceeding before the I.C.C. at Paris. Further the averments of the application dated 25.4.1992 do not indicate that the defendants submitted the application unequivocally rather subject to the supplying of the copy of plaint in Bangla and such fact also discloses from averments of the application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. As per order of the Court the copy of the plaint was submitted by the plaintiff in the Court in Bangla Language on 17.8.1992 and on that date the defendants also submitted application under section 34 of the Arbitration Act for staying the proceedings of the suit and as such it cannot be said that the defendants acquiesced with the cause of action before placing the plaint in Bangla in Court. The contents of the applications for time do not show that the defendant-appellants have abandoned its right under the arbitration agreement rather it has been indicated that they had no prior knowledge about the arbitration proceedings held at Paris, France as well as cause of action of the suit. So in view of the materials on record we hold that the defendants are not debarred from getting the advantage of section 34 of the Arbitration Act as they did not file written statements.

11. We have gone through all the decisions cited by both the parties and it is now well settled that a point like this can not be resolved by mere citation of the case. The facts of the present case are different from the facts of those cases which have been cited before us. No useful purpose would be served by discussing all the decisions in the instant case. However, we may refer to a decision in the case (Food Corporation of India and another versus Yadav Engineer and Contractor) reported in Supreme Court Cases 1982 (2SCC). In that case their Lordships observed as follows:-

"Under section 34 legislature by making it mandatory on the party seeking benefit of the arbitration agreement to apply for stay of the proceedings before filing the written statement or before taking any other steps in the proceedings, pointed out that filing of the written statement discloses such conduct on the part of the party as would unquestionably show that the party has abandoned its rights under the arbitration agreement and has disclosed an unequivocal intention to accept the forum of the Court for resolution of the dispute by waiving its right to get the dispute resolved by a forum contemplated by the arbitration agreement. When the party files written statement to the suit it discloses its defence, enters into a contest and invites the Court adjudicate upon the dispute. Once the Court is invited to adjudicate upon the dispute there is no question of them enforcing an arbitration agreement by forcing the parties to resort to the forum of their choice as set out in the arbitration agreement. This flows from the well-settled principle that the Court would normally hold the parties to the bargain."

<u>12. The law requires that if the arbitration clause exists in the agreement the Court should stay the proceedings of the suit and allow the parties to take the advantage of the agreement. As per arbitration clause the plaintiff resorted to the arbitration before the I.C.C. at Paris where we find these defendants were not made parties and for which they could not avail the advantage of arbitration. Article 18(2) of the contract indicates that the arbitration has to be held at Dhaka and since the defendants were not made parties before the I.C.C. they could not avail the advantage of the agreement. The position is that if the arbitration is held and the same could be fruit-fully concluded, in that case, the parties will be saved from unusual delay and expenses and if the dispute cannot be settled in the arbitration in that case the plaintiff is not debarred from prosecution. The whole purpose of section 34 of the Arbitration Act is to ensure that the parties to the agreement would honour the agreement to which they have subscribed from the beginning.</u>

13. It is found from the impugned judgment and order that the learned Subordinate Judge failed to notice that these defendants were not made parties in the arbitration proceeding before the I.C.C. at Paris and the plaint in Bangla filed in the Court on 17.8.1992 and on that date these defendants submitted application under section 34 of the Arbitration Act for staying the proceeding of the suit. It is also on record that the defendant-appellant did not file written statements.

14. In these circumstances and for the reasons stated above, we are of the opinion that the defendants did not take "steps in the proceedings" within the meaning of section 34 of the Arbitration Act and they are, therefore, entitled to an order of stay as prayed for by them. The learned Subordinate Judge appears to have acted illegally in rejecting the application of the defendant-appellants under section 34 of the Arbitration Act.

15. In the result, the appeal is, therefore, allowed without any order as to costs. The proceedings of Money Suit No. 1 of 1992 is stayed. The defendant-appellants are directed to take immediate steps for setting the dispute by referring the same to the appropriate arbitrator as contemplated by the arbitration clause in the agreement and the same should be completed within one year from the date of receipt of the record by the trial court failing which the suit shall proceed as usual.
